Drugs for preventing postoperative nausea and vomiting in adults afer
general anaesthesia: a network meta-analysis
Stephanie Weibel1, Gerta Rücker2, Leopold HJ Eberhart3, Nathan L Pace4, Hannah M Hartl1, Olivia L Jordan1, Debora Mayer1, Manuel
Riemer1, Maximilian S Schaefer5,6, Diana Raj7, Insa Backhaus8, Antonia Helf1, Tobias Schlesinger1, Peter Kienbaum5, Peter Kranke1
1Department of Anesthesiology and Critical Care, University Hospital Wuerzburg, Wuerzburg, Germany. 2Institute of Medical Biometry
and Statistics, Faculty of Medicine and Medical Center – University of Freiburg, Freiburg, Germany. 3Department of Anaesthesiology &
Intensive Care Medicine, Philipps-University Marburg, Marburg, Germany. 4Department of Anesthesiology, University of Utah, Salt Lake
City, UT, USA. 5Department of Anaesthesiology, University Hospital Düsseldorf, Düsseldorf, Germany. 6Department of Anesthesia, Critical
Care & Pain Medicine, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA. 7Department of Anaesthesia,
Intensive Care Medicine and Pain Medicine, Queen Elizabeth University Hospital, Glasgow, UK. 8Department of Public Health and
Infectious Diseases, Sapienza University of Rome, Rome, Italy
Contact: Peter Kranke, kranke_p@ukw.de.
Editorial group: Cochrane Anaesthesia Group.
Publication status and date: Edited (no change to conclusions), published in Issue 11, 2020.
Citation: Weibel S, Rücker G, Eberhart LHJ, Pace NL, Hartl HM, Jordan OL, Mayer D, Riemer M, Schaefer MS, Raj D, Backhaus I,
Helf A, Schlesinger T, Kienbaum P, Kranke P. Drugs for preventing postoperative nausea and vomiting in adults afer general
anaesthesia: a network meta-analysis. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2020, Issue 10. Art. No.: CD012859. DOI:

A B S T R A C T
Background
Postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) is a common adverse efect of anaesthesia and surgery. Up to 80% of patients may be afected.
These outcomes are a major cause of patient dissatisfaction and may lead to prolonged hospital stay and higher costs of care along with
more severe complications. Many antiemetic drugs are available for prophylaxis. They have various mechanisms of action and side efects,
but there is still uncertainty about which drugs are most efective with the fewest side efects.
Objectives
• To compare the eficacy and safety of diferent prophylactic pharmacologic interventions (antiemetic drugs) against no treatment, against
placebo, or against each other (as monotherapy or combination prophylaxis) for prevention of postoperative nausea and vomiting in adults
undergoing any type of surgery under general anaesthesia
• To generate a clinically useful ranking of antiemetic drugs (monotherapy and combination prophylaxis) based on eficacy and safety
• To identify the best dose or dose range of antiemetic drugs in terms of eficacy and safety
Search methods
We searched the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, Embase, the Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied
Health Literature (CINAHL), the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (WHO ICTRP), ClinicalTrials.gov,
and reference lists of relevant systematic reviews. The first search was performed in November 2017 and was updated in April 2020. In the
update of the search, 39 eligible studies were found that were not included in the analysis (listed as awaiting classification).

Selection criteria
Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing efectiveness or side efects of single antiemetic drugs in any dose or combination against
each other or against an inactive control in adults undergoing any type of surgery under general anaesthesia. All antiemetic drugs belonged
to one of the following substance classes: 5-HT3 receptor antagonists, D2 receptor antagonists, NK1 receptor antagonists, corticosteroids,
antihistamines, and anticholinergics. No language restrictions were applied. Abstract publications were excluded.
Data collection and analysis
A review team of 11 authors independently assessed trials for inclusion and risk of bias and subsequently extracted data. We performed
pair-wise meta-analyses for drugs of direct interest (amisulpride, aprepitant, casopitant, dexamethasone, dimenhydrinate, dolasetron,
droperidol, fosaprepitant, granisetron, haloperidol, meclizine, methylprednisolone, metoclopramide, ondansetron, palonosetron,
perphenazine, promethazine, ramosetron, rolapitant, scopolamine, and tropisetron) compared to placebo (inactive control). We
performed network meta-analyses (NMAs) to estimate the relative efects and ranking (with placebo as reference) of all available single
drugs and combinations. Primary outcomes were vomiting within 24 hours postoperatively, serious adverse events (SAEs), and any adverse
event (AE). Secondary outcomes were drug class-specific side efects (e.g. headache), mortality, early and late vomiting, nausea, and
complete response. We performed subgroup network meta-analysis with dose of drugs as a moderator variable using dose ranges based
on previous consensus recommendations. We assessed certainty of evidence of NMA treatment efects for all primary outcomes and drug
class-specific side efects according to GRADE (CINeMA, Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis). We restricted GRADE assessment to single
drugs of direct interest compared to placebo.
Main results
We included 585 studies (97,516 randomized participants). Most of these studies were small (median sample size of 100); they were
published between 1965 and 2017 and were primarily conducted in Asia (51%), Europe (25%), and North America (16%). Mean age of the
overall population was 42 years. Most participants were women (83%), had American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical status
I and II (70%), received perioperative opioids (88%), and underwent gynaecologic (32%) or gastrointestinal surgery (19%) under general
anaesthesia using volatile anaesthetics (88%).
In this review, 44 single drugs and 51 drug combinations were compared. Most studies investigated only single drugs (72%) and included
an inactive control arm (66%). The three most investigated single drugs in this review were ondansetron (246 studies), dexamethasone
(120 studies), and droperidol (97 studies).
Almost all studies (89%) reported at least one eficacy outcome relevant for this review. However, only 56% reported at least one relevant
safety outcome.
Altogether, 157 studies (27%) were assessed as having overall low risk of bias, 101 studies (17%) overall high risk of bias, and 327 studies
(56%) overall unclear risk of bias.
Vomiting within 24 hours postoperatively
Relative efects from NMA for vomiting within 24 hours (282 RCTs, 50,812 participants, 28 single drugs, and 36 drug combinations) suggest
that 29 out of 36 drug combinations and 10 out of 28 single drugs showed a clinically important benefit (defined as the upper end of the 95%
confidence interval (CI) below a risk ratio (RR) of 0.8) compared to placebo. Combinations of drugs were generally more efective than single
drugs in preventing vomiting. However, single NK1 receptor antagonists showed treatment efects similar to most of the drug combinations.
High-certainty evidence suggests that the following single drugs reduce vomiting (ordered by decreasing eficacy): aprepitant (RR 0.26, 95%
CI 0.18 to 0.38, high certainty, rank 3/28 of single drugs); ramosetron (RR 0.44, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.59, high certainty, rank 5/28); granisetron (RR
0.45, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.54, high certainty, rank 6/28); dexamethasone (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.57, high certainty, rank 8/28); and ondansetron
(RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.60, high certainty, rank 13/28). Moderate-certainty evidence suggests that the following single drugs probably
reduce vomiting: fosaprepitant (RR 0.06, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.21, moderate certainty, rank 1/28) and droperidol (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.69,
moderate certainty, rank 20/28).
Recommended and high doses of granisetron, dexamethasone, ondansetron, and droperidol showed clinically important benefit, but
low doses showed no clinically important benefit. Aprepitant was used mainly at high doses, ramosetron at recommended doses, and
fosaprepitant at doses of 150 mg (with no dose recommendation available).
Frequency of SAEs
Twenty-eight RCTs were included in the NMA for SAEs (10,766 participants, 13 single drugs, and eight drug combinations). The certainty of
evidence for SAEs when using one of the best and most reliable anti-vomiting drugs (aprepitant, ramosetron, granisetron, dexamethasone,
ondansetron, and droperidol compared to placebo) ranged from very low to low. Droperidol (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.08 to 9.71, low certainty,
rank 6/13) may reduce SAEs. We are uncertain about the efects of aprepitant (RR 1.39, 95% CI 0.26 to 7.36, very low certainty, rank 11/13),
ramosetron (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.05 to 15.74, very low certainty, rank 7/13), granisetron (RR 1.21, 95% CI 0.11 to 13.15, very low certainty, rank
10/13), dexamethasone (RR 1.16, 95% CI 0.28 to 4.85, very low certainty, rank 9/13), and ondansetron (RR 1.62, 95% CI 0.32 to 8.10, very
low certainty, rank 12/13). No studies reporting SAEs were available for fosaprepitant.

Frequency of any AE
Sixty-one RCTs were included in the NMA for any AE (19,423 participants, 15 single drugs, and 11 drug combinations). The certainty
of evidence for any AE when using one of the best and most reliable anti-vomiting drugs (aprepitant, ramosetron, granisetron,
dexamethasone, ondansetron, and droperidol compared to placebo) ranged from very low to moderate. Granisetron (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.80
to 1.05, moderate certainty, rank 7/15) probably has no or little efect on any AE. Dexamethasone (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.08, low certainty,
rank 2/15) and droperidol (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.98, low certainty, rank 6/15) may reduce any AE. Ondansetron (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.88 to
1.01, low certainty, rank 9/15) may have little or no efect on any AE. We are uncertain about the efects of aprepitant (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.78
to 0.97, very low certainty, rank 3/15) and ramosetron (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.54, very low certainty, rank 11/15) on any AE. No studies
reporting any AE were available for fosaprepitant.
Class-specific side efects
For class-specific side efects (headache, constipation, wound infection, extrapyramidal symptoms, sedation, arrhythmia, and QT
prolongation) of relevant substances, the certainty of evidence for the best and most reliable anti-vomiting drugs mostly ranged from very
low to low. Exceptions were that ondansetron probably increases headache (RR 1.16, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.28, moderate certainty, rank 18/23)
and probably reduces sedation (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.79 to 0.96, moderate certainty, rank 5/24) compared to placebo. The latter efect is limited
to recommended and high doses of ondansetron. Droperidol probably reduces headache (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.86, moderate certainty,
rank 5/23) compared to placebo. We have high-certainty evidence that dexamethasone (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.09, high certainty, rank
16/24) has no efect on sedation compared to placebo. No studies assessed substance class-specific side efects for fosaprepitant.
Direction and magnitude of network efect estimates together with level of evidence certainty are graphically summarized for all pre-
defined GRADE-relevant outcomes and all drugs of direct interest compared to placebo in http://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4066353.
Authors' conclusions
We found high-certainty evidence that five single drugs (aprepitant, ramosetron, granisetron, dexamethasone, and ondansetron) reduce
vomiting, and moderate-certainty evidence that two other single drugs (fosaprepitant and droperidol) probably reduce vomiting,
compared to placebo. Four of the six substance classes (5-HT3 receptor antagonists, D2 receptor antagonists, NK1 receptor antagonists, and
corticosteroids) were thus represented by at least one drug with important benefit for prevention of vomiting. Combinations of drugs were
generally more efective than the corresponding single drugs in preventing vomiting. NK1 receptor antagonists were the most efective drug
class and had comparable eficacy to most of the drug combinations. 5-HT3 receptor antagonists were the best studied substance class.
For most of the single drugs of direct interest, we found only very low to low certainty evidence for safety outcomes such as occurrence
of SAEs, any AE, and substance class-specific side efects.
Recommended and high doses of granisetron, dexamethasone, ondansetron, and droperidol were more efective than low doses for
prevention of vomiting. Dose dependency of side efects was rarely found due to the limited number of studies, except for the less sedating
efect of recommended and high doses of ondansetron.
The results of the review are transferable mainly to patients at higher risk of nausea and vomiting (i.e. healthy women undergoing
inhalational anaesthesia and receiving perioperative opioids). Overall study quality was limited, but certainty assessments of efect
estimates consider this limitation. No further eficacy studies are needed as there is evidence of moderate to high certainty for seven single
drugs with relevant benefit for prevention of vomiting. However, additional studies are needed to investigate potential side efects of these
drugs and to examine higher-risk patient populations (e.g. individuals with diabetes and heart disease).
P L A I N   L A N G U A G E   S U M M A R Y
Which medicines work best to prevent people from being sick (vomiting) afer an operation?
Why are people sick afer an operation?
Feeling sick (nausea) or being sick (vomiting) is a common unwanted efect of general anaesthesia—medicine that makes people
unconscious and unresponsive so they don't move or feel pain during an operation.
Most unwanted efects of general anaesthesia, including feeling or being sick, happen immediately and stop afer a few hours, although
some people may continue to feel sick for up to a day. If people carry on feeling or being sick, they might have to stay in hospital longer
than expected and may experience other unwanted efects or complications.
Women are more likely to be sick afer an operation, as are people taking opioid painkillers, those who have had motion sickness, and
those who have been sick afer previous operations.
Medicines to prevent people from being sick
Medicines called antiemetics are given to prevent people from feeling or being sick. These medicines may be given before or during
anaesthesia.

Antiemetic medicines are grouped into six main classes based on how they act. Combining medicines from diferent classes sometimes
makes them work better.
Why we did this Cochrane Review
We wanted to find out which medicines work best to prevent people from being sick afer an operation and cause the fewest unwanted
efects. Some unwanted efects of antiemetic medicines include headache, constipation, movement disorders such as tremors, sleepiness,
irregular heartbeat, and wound infection.
What did we do?
We searched for studies that looked at the use of antiemetic medicines in adults having general anaesthesia to prevent people from being
sick aferwards. 
We looked for randomized controlled studies, in which the treatments people received were decided at random. This type of study usually
gives the most reliable evidence about the efects of a treatment.
Search date
We included evidence published up to November 2017; in April 2020, we found another 39 studies, which are not yet included in the analysis.
What we found
We found 585 studies in 97,516 people who were given antiemetic medicines before or during general anaesthesia. People included in
the studies were more likely to be sick afer anaesthesia, as 83% were women and 88% were taking opioid painkillers. Most studies were
conducted in Asia, Europe, or North America.
These studies either measured how many people were sick in the first 24 hours afer their operation or how many unwanted efects were
reported, or both of these outcomes. Most studies compared medicines (given alone or in combination) with a dummy (placebo) treatment.
We compared all antiemetic medicines with each other using a mathematical method called network meta-analysis.
What were our main results and how reliable are these results?
Compared with placebo treatment, 10 out of 28 single medicines and 29 out of 36 combinations of medicines prevented people from being
sick in the first 24 hours afer their operation (282 studies). Combinations of antiemetic medicines generally worked better than single
medicines given alone. However, aprepitant, casopitant, and fosaprepitant worked as well alone as most combinations of antiemetics.
The single medicine that worked best in the ranking of all medicines was fosaprepitant, followed by casopitant, aprepitant, ramosetron,
granisetron, dexamethasone, tropisetron, ondansetron, dolasetron, and droperidol.
We are confident that aprepitant, ramosetron, granisetron, dexamethasone, and ondansetron prevent people from being sick. We are
moderately confident about how well fosaprepitant and droperidol work, but this finding may change when further evidence becomes
available. We are uncertain about how well casopitant, tropisetron, and dolasetron work.
Not all studies looked at serious, life-threatening unwanted efects. We are uncertain how many of these efects were reported when taking
an antiemetic medicine and whether serious, life-threatening unwanted efects occur at a similar rate or are reduced compared to placebo
(28 studies).
Of the best medicines with most reliable evidence for preventing being sick, granisetron and ondansetron probably made little to
no diference in the occurrence of unwanted efects compared to placebo, whereas dexamethasone and droperidol may cause fewer
unwanted efects than placebo. We are uncertain about unwanted efects with aprepitant and ramosetron (61 studies). We found no studies
looking at unwanted efects for fosaprepitant.
We are less confident about unwanted efects of other antiemetic medicines because we found little reliable evidence about this. Our
results for unwanted efects are likely to change when further evidence is available.
Conclusions
For people at higher risk, we found that some antiemetic medicines work well to prevent them from being sick afer general anaesthesia.
The best antiemetic medicines with reliable evidence were aprepitant, ramosetron, granisetron, dexamethasone, and ondansetron,
followed by fosaprepitant and droperidol.
However, we did not find enough reliable evidence about potential unwanted efects to rank these medicines reliably according to how
well they are tolerated.

B A C K G R O U N D
Description of the condition
Postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) is one of the major
and most frequently observed problems anaesthetists and patients
have to face afer surgical procedures. In the majority of cases,
PONV occurs during the first 24 hours postoperatively with a peak
in the immediate postoperative hours (Apfel 2002). About 30%
of all patients undergoing anaesthesia using volatile anaesthetics
without prior prophylaxis are afected by PONV afer surgery (Apfel
1999). In 1998, Apfel and colleagues developed a simplified score
that helps to predict individual risk for the occurrence of PONV
in adults. The four risk factors included are female gender, non-
smoker status, history of PONV or motion sickness, and expected
postoperative opioid use (Doleman 2018). Apfel suggests that the
likelihood of PONV ranges from 10% (no risk factors present) to 79%
(all four risk factors present) (Apfel 1999). The incidence of PONV
varies with a number of other factors,including hydration status
(Jewer 2019), type of anaesthetic (intravenous versus inhalational
(Miller 2018)) and possibly depth of anaesthesia (Lewis 2019). The
use of opioids can be avoided or minimised through the use of
regional anaesthetic techniques (Weinstein 2018) or systemic, non-
opioid analgesics such as lidocaine (Weibel 2018).
Rarely described but serious consequences of PONV that are
usually secondary to vomiting include aspiration pneumonia,
Boerhaave's syndrome, and severe subcutaneous emphysema
(Attalah 2004; Baric 2000; Kranke 2011; Reddy 2008; Schumann
1999). However, PONV is itself an unpleasant and uncomfortable
feeling and a burdensome side efect for patients receiving
anaesthesia (Kranke 2011). It is subjectively rated to be as serious as
postoperative pain and has an important influence on the quality of
recovery (Hocking 2013; Kranke 2011). Moreover, PONV can lead to
a prolonged or unexpected hospital stay, or even to re-admission.
It also interferes with early postoperative recovery (Kranke 2011).
Description of the intervention
A large variety of antiemetic drugs—grouped into six diferent drug
classes—are available for prevention of PONV (Gan 2007a; Gan
2014; Horn 2014; Wiesmann 2015): 5-HT3 receptor antagonists (e.g.
ondansetron, dolasetron, granisetron, tropisetron, ramosetron,
palonosetron); 
D2 
receptor 
antagonists 
(e.g. 
droperidol,
haloperidol, 
metoclopramide, 
perphenazine, 
amisulpride,
alizapride, chlorpromazine, domperidone, prochlorperazine,
sulpiride, 
trimethobenzamide); 
NK1 
receptor 
antagonists
(e.g. 
aprepitant, 
casopitant, 
rolapitant, 
fosaprepitant,
CP-122,721, vestipitant); corticosteroids (e.g. dexamethasone,
methylprednisolone, 
betamethasone); 
antihistamines 
(e.g.
dimenhydrinate, 
meclizine, 
promethazine, 
cyclizine); 
and
anticholinergics (i.e. scopolamine).
The six diferent substance classes are characterized by varying
adverse efects: 5-HT3 receptor antagonists (e.g. headache,
constipation), D2 receptor antagonists (e.g. extrapyramidal
symptoms, sedation, arrhythmia, QT prolongation), corticosteroids
(e.g. 
hyperglycaemia, 
immunosuppression, 
wound 
healing
deficits), antihistamines (e.g. drowsiness, xerostomia, urinary
tract dificulties), and anticholinergics (e.g. dry mouth, visual
disturbances) (Gan 2014; Horn 2014; Wiesmann 2015). Currently
limited evidence is available on adverse efects arising from NK1
receptor antagonists. However, increased dizziness or headache
was described by individual studies (Diemunsch 2009).
Drugs with diferent mechanisms of action should be used in
combination to optimize eficacy (Gan 2007b). For example, the
5-HT3 antagonists, which have better anti-vomiting than anti-
nausea eficacy (although associated with headache), can be used
in combination with droperidol, which has greater anti-nausea
eficacy and a protective efect against headache (Gan 2007b).
In addition to drugs with direct antiemetic action, several other
strategies for PONV prophylaxis are available such as use of drugs
with indirect opioid-sparing efects (e.g. gabapentin; Grant 2016), or
strategies such as reducing the emetic potency of the anaesthesia
itself (e.g. by using propofol; Apfel 2004), or non-pharmacologic
prophylaxis strategies (e.g. stimulation of the wrist acupuncture
point PC6; Lee 2015). These strategies are not within the focus of
the current review.
Gan 2014 in its 'Consensus guidelines for the management of
postoperative nausea and vomiting' provides information about
current options for prevention and treatment of PONV including
both pharmacologic and non-pharmacologic regimens comprising
the most commonly used antiemetic drugs, doses, and timing of
application. With adequate prophylaxis, one antiemetic agent can
reduce the likelihood (relative reduction) of PONV by 25% (Gan
2014). This evidence-based guideline currently recommends one to
two interventions for PONV prophylaxis for patients at moderate
risk (Gan 2014).
It is important to provide adequate prophylaxis with regard to the
type and time of application. Intravenous or parenteral application
of antiemetics in accordance with their pharmacokinetic profile
may be appropriate for mitigating the risk of the varying duration
of surgery and the need for a reasonably efective drug level at
the 'time of risk' in the postoperative setting. A large majority of
antiemetic drugs are usually administered by a slow intravenous
push or as an infusion administered over a short time. Although
some 'alternative' therapies are available (e.g. aromatherapy
(Hines 2018)), this review does not include such substances.
How the intervention might work
Five of the six substance classes with direct antiemetic efects difer
mostly in their antagonistic action against diferent emetogenic
substances at specific receptors, for example, in the area postrema
or on the free nerve endings of the vagus nerve (Gan 2007a; Gan
2014; Horn 2014; Wiesmann 2015).
•
5-HT3 receptor antagonists: high levels of the neurotransmitter
serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, 5-HT) induce nausea and
vomiting by activating specific receptors in the gut and central
nervous system. Drugs belonging to this substance class inhibit
serotonin receptors centrally and peripherally.
•
D2 receptor antagonists: dopamine antagonists work as
antiemetics in small dosages by blocking central dopamine
receptors.
•
NK1 receptor antagonists: the neurotransmitter substance P
binds to the neurokinin 1-receptor in the area postrema and
thereby induces nausea and vomiting. NK1 receptor antagonists
block these receptors and inhibit this pathway.
•

A sixth group of antiemetics with direct antiemetic efects
consists of corticosteroids. It is not known with any certainty
how corticosteroids exert their antiemetic efects. Some theories
assume that the anti-inflammatory impact and the decrease in
arachidonic acid release reduce the occurrence of PONV.
Why it is important to do this review
Preventing PONV is important for the well-being of patients and is
a major factor influencing patients’ satisfaction with anaesthesia.
It is therefore important for patients to be provided with suficient
antiemetic prophylaxis. PONV is also a major contributor to direct
and indirect healthcare costs (Eberhart 2014; Hirsch 1994). Amongst
others, these include costs for prolonged stays in recovery rooms
and costs of extra nursing time (Hirsch 1994; Smith 2012). In times
when healthcare resources are scarce and the healthcare workforce
is decreasing, the correct prophylaxis ofers an advantage. Many
antiemetics have proven eficacy for clinical use. Unfortunately, the
use of prophylactic antiemetics for patients at risk is not part of the
daily routine of all anaesthetists due to inadequate implementation
of the risk-adapted approach in some clinical departments (Franck
2010). Moreover, risk‒benefit issues remain a topic of debate in the
anaesthesia community, and the fear of possible adverse efects
(Weibel 2018) may be another reason for restraint (Kranke 2011).
Many studies have investigated not only monotherapies but
also combinations of antiemetics to reduce the likelihood of
developing PONV. Trials examining diferent doses or dose ranges
of one or more drugs administered in various ways (intravenous,
intramuscular, oral, or transdermal) create a wide spectrum of
information that is dificult to assess by simple direct comparisons.
In 2006, Carlisle and Stevenson performed a systematic review
that assessed all available drugs with antiemetic action for
preventing PONV in adults and children in terms of eficacy
and side efects. This review included more than 700 studies
with over 100,000 participants (Carlisle 2006a). All trials reporting
PONV as an outcome and comparing a drug with placebo, no
treatment, or another drug, or comparing diferent dosing or timing
of administration, were included. This review contained a large
number of direct comparisons, as no restrictions regarding study
population or type of intervention were defined.
Tricco and colleagues published a systematic review with network
meta-analysis (NMA) of the eficacy and safety of serotonin receptor
antagonists compared to each other, compared to placebo, and
in combination with other antiemetic agents for PONV prevention
(Tricco 2015a; Tricco 2015b). However, these review authors
examined no other substance classes.
Despite the continuing flow of clinical trials on PONV prophylaxis,
there is still no current overview of all relevant substance classes.
There is a shortage of direct comparisons of frequently used
antiemetics, and a clinically useful ranking of all antiemetic
drugs with respect to both eficacy and safety is lacking. The
Carlisle review of PONV needs to be updated (Carlisle 2006a).
However, the original review was withdrawn in 2017, in part
because several studies that had been included were retracted
since publication (Carlisle 2017). Another reason for withdrawal
was that the literature is now so large and complex that a very large
series of direct comparisons—as performed in the Carlisle review
of PONV—would create an overwhelmingly burdensome task and
would be very dificult to comprehend. Therefore, a new and
more eficient approach was needed to allow readers to appreciate
readily the best-quality evidence available. For the current review,
we performed an NMA that allows comparison of antiemetic drugs
in a direct and indirect manner (see Methods). The aim of this
review is to generate a clinically useful ranking of antiemetic
drugs (monotherapy and combination prophylaxis). This review
also seeks to provide clear information for patients and physicians
to guide clinical decisions that enhance treatment eficacy and
reduce the occurrence of side efects. To enhance the feasibility,
we made a pre hoc decision to focus on the six clinically relevant
drug classes with direct antiemetic action currently used or under
investigation. Drugs such as gabapentin, which exert an antiemetic
efect in an indirect way via an opioid-sparing efect (Grant 2016), as
well as non-pharmacologic interventions (Lee 2015), are not within
the scope of this review. This systematic review is deliberately
designed to address some of the questions raised by the current
PONV guideline (Gan 2014), with the aim of providing an evidence-
based basis for future updates to this guideline.
O B J E C T I V E S
•
To compare the eficacy and safety of diferent prophylactic
pharmacologic interventions (antiemetic drugs) against no
treatment, against placebo, or against each other (as
monotherapy or combination prophylaxis) for prevention of
postoperative nausea and vomiting in adults undergoing any
type of surgery under general anaesthesia
•
To generate a clinically useful ranking of antiemetic drugs
(monotherapy and combination prophylaxis) based on eficacy
and safety
•
To identify the best dose or dose range of antiemetic drugs in
terms of eficacy and safety
M E T H O D S
Criteria for considering studies for this review
Types of studies
In this review, we included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that
compare one or more antiemetics for prevention of PONV against
no treatment, placebo, or another antiemetic drug. We excluded
quasi-randomized trials (i.e. trials in which treatment allocation
is achieved by date of birth, alternation, or similar predictable
methods), cluster-randomized trials, and cross-over studies.
We included trials in which allocation to treatment may not
have been adequately concealed, but we considered trial
methodological quality in data analyses and interpretation.
We did not restrict inclusion of studies based on language of
publication.
Retracted studies and studies authored by Fujii and colleagues were
not included in the review (Kranke 2000; Tramer 2013).

Eligible studies must have been reported as full-text journal
publications or comprehensive study reports. Because we expected
to identify more than 1000 full-text studies, we excluded studies
published in abstract form only to reduce the workload and to
enhance the feasibility of completing the review in a reasonable
time frame.
Types of participants
We included only trials that analysed adult participants (i.e. the
majority of participants over 18 years of age) undergoing any type
of surgery under general anaesthesia. We did not include studies
using regional or sedative anaesthetic techniques.
Types of interventions
We included studies that compared any pharmacologic
intervention(s) with antiemetic action belonging to one of the
following drug classes versus each other or versus no treatment, or
versus placebo.
•
5-HT3 receptor antagonists.
•
D2 receptor antagonists.
•
NK1 receptor antagonists.
•
Corticosteroids.
•
Antihistamines (histamine 1 receptor antagonists).
•
Anticholinergics.
For future updates, we may include emerging drugs from other
drug classes if it has been demonstrated that they exert a direct
antiemetic action.
We also included trials that analysed combinations of antiemetic
drugs, whereby each combination represents a separate
intervention of interest and therefore a separate node in the NMA
(splitting). In the run-up to the NMA, we assessed the geometry
of the network (all interventions (monotherapy and combination
prophylaxis) versus monoprophylaxis alone). We aimed to examine
all possible combination prophylaxis treatments in cases where
the geometry of the network allowed this holistic approach. All
networks in the current review were well connected.
Diferent doses of drugs were combined into one node (lumping).
Dose efects were analysed in subgroup analyses, especially in
cases of heterogeneity or inconsistency.
Not all eligible interventions from the various drug classes were
of direct (primary) interest. All drugs of direct interest for the
review with highest clinical relevance are listed in the section
"Interventions of direct interest". Eligible interventions not of direct
interest were included in the network to increase the amount of
available (indirect) information in the analysis (see "Inclusion of
additional interventions to supplement the analysis") (Ades 2013;
Protocol Template 2014).
For inclusion, the antiemetic drug(s) had to have been
administered before the onset of PONV. These drug(s) could have
been given preoperatively, at induction of anaesthesia, or during
anaesthesia.
Participants in all treatment arms within a study must have
been subject to the same anaesthesia regimen with comparable
dosing because the anaesthesia management itself may have an
influence on the incidence of PONV. For studies that reported
results separately for varying baseline anaesthesia regimens, the
diferent regimens were not combined but were considered as sub-
studies.
We assumed that, in principle, any participant meeting the
inclusion criteria could be selected at random for one of the eligible
interventions.
Interventions of direct interest
Antiemetic drugs of direct interest in the current review include
those recommended in the "Consensus guidelines for the

published in the last five years before the search date (2017). In

Types of outcome measures
Studies must have reported at least one of the following primary or
secondary outcomes to be fully eligible for and to be included in the
review. Reporting of outcomes of interest was an essential eligibility
criterion to enhance the feasibility of the review workload.
Primary outcomes
We estimated the relative efects of competing interventions
according to the following primary outcomes.
•
Vomiting (or dry retching) within 24 hours: number of
participants with events within 0 to 24 hours (± 6 hours)
postoperatively.
•
Serious adverse events (SAEs): number of participants with at
least one SAE (as defined in the study) in the observation period
(up to seven days).
•
Any adverse event (AE): number of participants with at least one
AE (as defined in the study) in the observation period (up to
seven days).
Secondary outcomes
We estimated the relative efects of competing interventions
according to the following secondary outcomes.
Substance class-specific side efects
•
Headache: number of participants with headache in the
observation period (up to seven days)
•
Sedation/drowsiness: number of participants with sedation/
drowsiness in the observation period (up to seven days)
•
Extrapyramidal symptoms: number of participants with
extrapyramidal symptoms (e.g. dystonia, dyskinesia, akathisia,
bradykinesia, tremor) in the observation period (up to seven
days)
•
Constipation: number of participants with constipation in the
observation period (up to seven days)
•
Postoperative wound infection: number of participants with
postoperative wound infection in the observation period (up to
seven days)
•
Arrhythmia: number of participants with an arrhythmia (as
defined by triallists) in the observation period (up to seven days)
•
Visual disturbances: number of participants with visual
disturbances (e.g. blurred vision) in the observation period (up
to seven days)
•
QT prolongation: number of participants with a QT prolongation
(as defined by triallists) in the observation period (up to seven
days)
Other secondary outcomes
•
Mortality: number of participants who have died in the
observation period (up to seven days)
•
Early postoperative vomiting (or dry retching): number of
participants with events within an observation period starting
immediately afer anaesthesia and ending two to six hours later
(or defined as occurring in the postanaesthesia care unit (PACU))
•
Late postoperative vomiting (or dry retching): number of
participants with events within an observation period within
the range of two to 24 hours postoperatively. If studies have
recorded the outcome during diferent periods of the two to 24
hour postoperative period but have not reported the risk for
the complete observation period (two to 24 hours), we reported
the risk of the outcome once for each study using the risk for
the period in which the outcome was most common (all groups
combined)
•
Nausea within 24 hours postoperatively (0 to 24 hours ± 6 hours):
studies that have reported the combined endpoint PONV only
(and not nausea separately) were considered as nausea. We did
not include in the analysis continuous data on nausea (such as
grades of nausea measured on appropriate scales)
•
Complete response: number of participants without vomiting,
nausea, or any need for rescue treatment within 24 hours
postoperatively
Search methods for identification of studies
We searched for all kinds of comparisons involving the research
question.
Electronic searches
We identified RCTs through literature searching designed to identify
relevant trials, as outlined in Chapter 4 of the Cochrane Handbook
for Systematic Reviews of Interventions (Lefebvre 2019). We did not
apply language restrictions.
We searched the following databases for relevant trials (first search
2017 November 6, update search 2020 April 23).
•
Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL; 2020,
Issue 4).
•
MEDLINE (Ovid SP, 1946 to 2020 April 20).
•
Embase (Ovid SP, 1974 to 2020 April 20).
•
Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature
(CINAHL) via EBSCO host (1982 to 2020 April 20).
We developed a draf search strategy for MEDLINE, which we used
as the basis for the search strategies applied in the other databases
listed. These search strategies can be found in Appendix 1.
We scanned the following trials registries for study reports and
protocols, and for ongoing and unpublished trials.
•
ClinicalTrials.gov (2 November 2017).
•
World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry
Platform (WHO ICTRP) (3 November 2017).
In the updated search in 2020, the study registries were
not searched. Records of the ClinicalTrial.gov and WHO ICTRP
databases were systematically added to CENTRAL, starting in
August 2017 and April 2019. These records are therefore covered
in the updated CENTRAL search. The WHO ICTRP trial register was
closed at the date of the update search because of COVID-19.
Therefore, the WHO ICTRP search is currently not complete.
All included trials have been checked against the Retraction Watch
database (November 2018).
Searching other resources
We scanned the reference lists of relevant systematic reviews for
additional trials (Carlisle 2006a; De Oliveira 2013; Liu 2015; Tricco
2015a; Tricco 2015b).

Data collection and analysis
Selection of studies
We used Covidence, a web-based sofware platform (Covidence),
for the process of study selection. All records identified by the
search strategy described above were imported into Covidence.
The following review authors participated in the screening of
records: SW, DM, MR, HH, AH, PKr, IB, DR, LE, MS, and TS. In each
case, two of them independently screened the title and abstract
of an individual record for eligibility using a pre-defined eligibility
checklist (Appendix 2). For all potentially relevant records, we
retrieved the full texts before making the final decision about
which studies satisfied the inclusion criteria. When necessary, we
contacted trial authors for missing information (18 requests sent
to authors; none answered). All full texts were reviewed by two
independent review authors. We resolved any discrepancies in
judgement by discussion with a third review author (SW, PKr).
Data extraction and management
Two independent review authors extracted the data using a
pre-defined data extraction form in the Covidence environment
(Appendix 3; Covidence). Extracted data included data on outcomes
and potential efect modifiers, along with other data. The following
review authors participated in data extraction: SW, DM, MR, HH, AH,
PKr, IB, DR, LE, and MS. A third review author (SW) checked all data
extraction forms and resolved any discrepancies. When necessary,
we contacted trial authors to request missing information (17
requests sent to authors; seven provided data). We exported
data from Covidence into Review Manager sofware and Excel
spreadsheets, and we checked them for accuracy (SW, OJ) (Review
Manager 2014).
Basic study characteristics
We extracted from each included study data on the following
additional information.
•
Identification (year of publication; journal; first author (with
contact information); location of study conduct; number of
centres; duration of study; and trial registry number).
•
Methods (study design and groups).
•
Population details (inclusion and exclusion criteria with group
diferences; and participant flow (number of participants
assessed for eligibility, number randomized, number that
received treatment, and number analysed)).
•
Prognostic variables (population and baseline characteristics,
risk factors for PONV: gender; smoking status; history of PONV/
motion sickness; type of surgery; type of anaesthesia; duration
of anaesthesia; and use of perioperative opioids).
Outcome data
We extracted from each included study all data relevant to the
primary and secondary outcomes listed in the section Types of
outcome measures.
We extracted the following characteristics associated with
monitoring and reporting of (severe) adverse events in each
primary study.
•
Type of monitoring for SAEs/AEs (active or passive).
•
Types of AEs (defined AEs or any AEs).
•
Use of an accepted international classification for SAEs (e.g.
according to the International Council for Harmonisation of
Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use
(ICH) guidelines).
•
Number of SAEs reported (yes or no).
Data on potential efect modifiers
From each included study, we extracted data on the following
potential efect modifiers.
•
Intervention (dose; time point of administration (early versus
late (afer incision)); and route of administration).
•
Risk of bias (sequence generation; blinding of participant,
personnel, and outcome assessors; and incomplete outcome
data).
•
Funding source (sponsorship source and involvement).
Assessment of risk of bias in included studies
We assessed the risk of bias for each included study by using
the Cochrane 'Risk of bias' assessment tool 1.0 (Higgins 2011).
Standard items include random sequence generation, allocation
concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of
outcome assessors, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting,
and any other bias. We judged each item as being at 'low risk of
bias', 'high risk of bias', or 'unclear risk of bias'. We included a ‘Risk
of bias’ table as part of the Characteristics of included studies table
and the ‘Risk of bias summary’/‘Risk of bias graph’ figures, which
detailed all of the judgements made for all studies included in the
review.
We also assessed the characteristics associated with monitoring
and reporting of severe and any adverse events in each
primary study and reported this information in an additional
table—"Assessment of adverse event monitoring"—along with a
judgement on the risk of bias as described by Tramacere and
colleagues (Tramacere 2015).
Two review authors independently performed study quality
assessment using a pre-defined critical appraisal form in
the Covidence environment (Appendix 4). We resolved any
disagreements by discussion with a third review author (SW).
Random sequence generation
We considered sequence generation as adequate if it was generated
by a random system (i.e. a computer, a random number table
algorithm, or tossing of a coin). We considered sequence generation
inadequate if a non-random system was used (i.e. names or
dates). We excluded quasi-randomized trials. We assessed the
study as having ‘unclear risk of bias’ if the only information on
randomization was a statement that the study was randomized.
Allocation concealment
We considered concealment adequate if an acceptable method
was used to ensure that group assignment was not revealed
to patient recruiters, investigators, or participants before final
allocation into the respective group. Acceptable methods included
a central allocation system, sequentially numbered sealed opaque
envelopes (SNOSEs), or an on-site locked computer. We considered
concealment to be inadequate if it allowed patient recruiters,
investigators, or participants to know the treatment allocation in
advance. We assessed the study as having ‘unclear risk of bias’ if

the concealment procedure was not reported or was not suficiently

Blinding of participants and personnel outcome assessors
We considered blinding adequate if all participants and personnel
(e.g. anaesthetists) were blinded to the intervention. We considered
blinding inadequate if participants and personnel were not blinded
to the intervention. We assessed the study as having ‘unclear risk
of bias’ if study authors stated only that the study was blinded and
if it remained unclear who was blinded.
Blinding of outcome assessors
We considered blinding adequate if all outcome assessors were
blinded to the intervention. We considered blinding inadequate
if outcome assessors were not blinded to the intervention. We
assessed the study as having ‘unclear risk of bias’ if study authors
stated only that the study was blinded and if it remained unclear
who was blinded.
Incomplete outcome data
We considered the domain ‘incomplete outcome data’ as adequate
if the number of dropouts was 15% or less and was balanced
between arms, and if the reasons for dropout were reported and
appeared to be unrelated to the studied outcomes. We considered
outcome data as incomplete if the number of dropouts was greater
than 15% or was significantly imbalanced between groups, or if the
reasons for dropout were not reported or appeared to be related
to outcomes of interest in the study. We assessed the study as
having ‘unclear risk of bias’ if details on the number of dropouts and
reasons for dropout were not suficiently reported.
Selective outcome reporting
We assessed selective outcome reporting by comparing the type
and order of outcomes (primary versus secondary) reported in the
study protocol, along with the published outcomes. We considered
outcome reporting as adequate if a prospectively registered study
protocol was available, and if all primary and secondary outcomes
were also reported in the published study as prespecified in the
protocol. We judged selective outcome reporting as having 'high
risk of bias' if the pre-defined primary outcomes in the registered
protocol difered from those in the published study report. If no
prospectively registered study protocol was available, we assessed
selective outcome reporting as having 'unclear risk of bias'.
Other sources of bias
Other potential risks of bias included baseline imbalance in
population characteristics and risk factors for PONV (prognostic
variables) within studies that are strongly related to outcome
measures and therefore may cause bias in the intervention efect
estimate. An imbalance was defined as either a 20% diference
between groups or P < 0.05 for a diference between two groups, if
reported in the study. We assessed the study as having ‘unclear risk
of other bias’ if details on baseline characteristics or risk factors for
PONV were not suficiently reported.
Overall risk of bias summary
We summarized the risk of bias for each study by referring to
judgements for the most important domains 'sequence generation',
'blinding of participant, personnel, and outcome assessors', and
'incomplete outcome data'. We did not include in the overall
risk of bias summary the domains 'allocation concealment' (for
explanation, see Diferences between protocol and review),
'selective outcome reporting', and 'other sources of bias'. The
review included studies published over a time span of 50 years,
and judgements on the domains 'selective outcome reporting' and
'other sources of bias' strongly depend on the year the study was
conducted. Older studies (before 2000) were not registered in trial
registries, and risk factors for PONV were not specified at older
dates. We performed sensitivity analyses with information from the
domain 'other sources of bias'.
We classified each study as having 'low risk of overall bias' when we
judged all relevant domains as having 'low risk of bias'. If we judged
at least one domain as having 'high risk of bias' or all domains
as having 'unclear risk of bias', we classified overall risk of bias
for the study as 'high risk of overall bias'. In the remaining cases,
we classified the study as having 'unclear risk of overall bias'. We
used information from the 'overall risk of bias summary' when
performing sensitivity analyses.
Assessment of adverse event monitoring
The way of monitoring adverse events may introduce bias to the
relevant adverse outcomes. Therefore, we assessed the risk of bias
associated with monitoring for adverse events. We evaluated the
methods of monitoring for adverse events in each primary study on
the basis of the following questions as described by Tramacere and
colleagues with some modifications (Tramacere 2015).
•
Any AE.
◦ Did the authors pro-actively monitor for any AE?
◦ Did the authors simply provide spontaneous reporting
(passively) of AEs by participants?
◦ Did the authors report all relevant (class-specific) AEs?
•
SAEs.
◦ Did the authors define SAEs according to an accepted
international classification?
We did not include this information in the ‘Risk of bias’ table. We
reported this information in an additional table ‘Monitoring and
reporting of any (severe) adverse events’, along with a judgement
of the risk of bias (Tramacere 2015).
We used information from the assessment of adverse event
monitoring to test the robustness of efect estimates for the primary
outcomes ‘SAEs’ and ‘any AE’ by sensitivity analyses (exclusion of
'high and unclear risk of bias' studies for adverse event monitoring).
Review of network geometry
We graphically evaluated the geometry of the whole network
including interventions of direct interest (monotherapy and
combination prophylaxis) and any other intervention in which
we were not directly interested (see ‘Additional interventions to
supplement the analysis') using the function netgraph of the R
package netmeta (Rücker 2016; netmeta). We used the information
from the network geometry to determine whether a network meta-
analysis was feasible for all interventions or only for sub-networks
(e.g. monoprophylaxis). The network is laid out in the plane as
a circle, where the nodes in the graph layout correspond to the
treatments and edges display the observed (direct) treatment
comparisons. The thickness of the edges is proportionate to the
number of included studies comparing two treatments.

Measures of treatment efect
Relative treatment efects
We estimated the pair-wise relative treatment efects of competing
interventions using the risk ratio (RR) with 95% confidence intervals
(95% CIs) for each outcome.
Results from network meta-analyses were presented as summary
relative efects (RR) for each possible pair of treatments.
Relative treatment ranking
We ranked competing treatments by P scores (Rücker 2015), using
the function netrank of the R package netmeta (netmeta). We used
this method to measure the extent of certainty that a treatment
is better than another treatment, averaged over all competing
treatments (Rücker 2015). P scores should not be confused with P
values. P scores are the frequentist analogue and are numerically
similar to Bayesian surface under the cumulative ranking curve
(SUCRA) values (Rücker 2015). P scores are ranking numbers
between 0 and 1 that are derived from the P values of all pair-wise
comparisons. Treatments are ranked from best to worst according
to decreasing P scores for all outcomes with the exception of
complete response (increasing P scores).
We looked at comparative eficacies between antiemetic drugs and
expressed this finding using placebo as the reference intervention
and presented the results in forest plots. We ranked treatment
efects in forest plots according to P scores in decreasing order (the
most efective intervention is presented at the top).
Size of efects
We used clinically relevant size of efects rather than
statistical significance to describe network meta-analysis estimates
(Nikolakopoulou 2019 Wasserstein 2019). For eficacy outcomes
such as prevention of vomiting or nausea, we defined the clinically
important size of benefit as RR of 0.80 and the reciprocal as
clinically important harm (RR 1.25). Efects lower than 0.80 and
larger than 1.25 were considered to be clinically important. The
range between 0.8 and 1.25 was termed the ‘range of equivalence’,
which included unimportant treatment efects (Nikolakopoulou
2019). The relative position of the point estimates indicated the
direction of the efect as ‘benefit’, ‘no or minimal efect’, or
‘harm’ (Figure 1). The extent of the 95% CI indicated the certainty
of the estimated efect as ‘important’ or as ‘associated with
uncertainty’ (Figure 1).

Unit of analysis issues
Cluster-randomized trials
We did not include cluster-randomized trials.
Cross-over trials
We did not include trials with cross-over design.
Studies with multiple treatment groups
We included multi-arm studies in the data set as a series of two-
arm comparisons. To reflect the fact that comparisons within multi-
arm studies are correlated, we adjusted the standard error of each
two-arm comparison from a multi-arm study. We used the method
proposed by Rücker and Schwarzer, which uses back-calculated
standard errors in the weighted least-square estimator to reflect the
within-study correlation (Rücker 2012; Rücker 2014; Rücker 2015).
Studies with zero events
We included in the analysis studies with zero events in one or more
arms. We applied the constant continuity correction approach
(continuity correction 0.5) as described by Sweeting 2004, using the
R package netmeta version 1.0-1 for analysis (netmeta).
Dealing with missing data
We noted levels of attrition for included studies in the ‘Risk of
bias’ table as part of the Characteristics of included studies. We did
not request from trial authors missing participant outcome data to
reduce the workload and to enhance the feasibility of the review
being completed in a reasonable time frame.
We carried out analyses for eficacy outcomes, as far as possible,
on an intention-to-treat (ITT) basis. For the analysis of safety, we
carried out as-treated analysis as far as possible (and we were ready
to accept if the randomization was broken).
In cases of missing data, we used an 'available-case analysis' by
excluding from the analysis all participants for whom the outcome
is missing.
Assessment of heterogeneity
Assessment of clinical and methodological heterogeneity within
treatment comparisons
We planned to use descriptive statistics of parameters reported in
the Characteristics of included studies table to assess whether the
studies within each pair-wise comparison are homogenous enough
with respect to potential efect modifiers (such as risk of bias,
intervention details, and funding source), so that the assumption
of homogeneity might be plausible. For the efect modifiers ‘risk
of bias’ and ‘dose of intervention’, we accepted heterogeneity
(see inclusion criteria of this review) and assessed the impact of
these efect modifiers via sensitivity analysis for ‘risk of bias’ and
subgroup analysis for ‘dose of intervention’. Due to the quantity of
data and the lack of information for the efect modifier ‘funding
source’ in many studies, an objective and reliable assessment of
the distribution of this efect modifier within all comparisons was
not possible. In general, we assumed that for all included studies,
the study populations, interventions, outcomes, and study settings
matched the inclusion criteria of the current systematic review.
Assessment of transitivity across treatment comparisons
We planned to assess the assumption of transitivity by comparing
the distribution of potential efect modifiers (see Appendix
3: ‘Potential efect modifiers’) across the diferent pair-wise
comparisons. In the case of intransitivity (e.g. substantially
imbalanced distribution of efect modifiers among comparisons),

Assessment of reporting biases
When we identified 10 or more relevant studies, we investigated risk
of bias across studies (such as publication bias) in pair-wise meta-
analyses ('Interventions of direct interest', primary outcomes) using
funnel plots. If funnel plot asymmetry was suggested by a visual
assessment, we performed exploratory analyses (e.g. Rücker’s
arcsine test for dichotomous data, contour-enhanced funnel plots,
trim and fill sensitivity analyses) to further investigate funnel plot
asymmetry. We analysed reporting bias using the R package meta
version 4.9-7 (meta).
Data synthesis
We used standard pair-wise meta-analysis and NMA for
synthesizing information from numerous studies addressing the
same outcomes but involving diferent interventions.
Methods for pair-wise meta-analyses and network meta-
analyses
We performed standard pair-wise meta-analyses for all primary
outcomes and substance class-specific side efects using a random-
efects model (inverse variance weighting) in RevMan for each
treatment comparison (drugs of primary interest versus placebo)
with at least two studies. We reported the results in the Data
and analyses section. We did not report the results in the Efects
of interventions section to reduce the amount of information
presented.
For NMAs, we used a frequentist approach based on the graph-
theoretical method of Rücker et al (Rücker 2012). We performed
random-efects NMAs for all outcomes in R using the package
netmeta version 1.0-1 (netmeta; Rücker 2014). We separated mixed
treatment evidence into direct and indirect evidence using the
function netsplit from this package.
We reported all NMA, direct, and indirect estimates of all outcomes
in supplementary files to reduce the amount of information
provided in the text. In the Efects of interventions section, we
presented only the following selection of NMA estimates of the
primary analyses on the outcome level. First, we summarized
the range of NMA efects for both drug combinations and single
drugs with important clinical efects. Second, we summarized the
range of NMA efects of all drug combinations and all single drugs
(independent of the direction of efects). In the range of efects,
we specified the most efective and the least efective drug or drug
combination.
Methods for analysing additive efects of drug combinations
The primary NMA treated all single drugs and all combination
prophylaxes as diferent nodes in the network. We performed
a second analysis based on the assumption that the efects of
combined treatments (e.g. A + B, A + B + C, B + C) are additive sums
of their components. This assumption, together with the network
structure, leads to a statistical model that allows decomposing
the observed relative efects into the single components and
estimating the efects of the components. The hypothesis of
additivity can be tested by comparing estimates from this model
with those from the primary analysis (Mills 2012). We used the
function netcomb of the R package netmeta version 1.0-1 for
analysis (netmeta; Rücker 2019).
Subgroup analysis and investigation of heterogeneity
Assessment of statistical heterogeneity
Assumptions when estimating the heterogeneity
In NMA, we assumed the same heterogeneity across the diferent
comparisons. In standard pair-wise meta-analyses, we assumed the
common heterogeneity variance estimated from the NMA for each
pair-wise comparison.
Measures and tests for heterogeneity
We assessed heterogeneity by the common between-trial variance
measure (tau2), the Q-statistics, the I2 statistic, and the 95%
prediction interval (95% PI). The 95% PI shows where the true efect
of a new study similar to the existing studies is expected to lie (Riley
2011). For interpretation of heterogeneity, we compared the 95% PI
and the 95% CI of the NMA treatment estimate with respect to the
range of clinically relevant efect sizes and the range of equivalence.
Assessment of statistical inconsistency (incoherence)
Inconsistency (incoherence) is the statistical manifestation of
intransitivity that occurs when the direct and indirect estimates
in a network of treatments do not agree. The distinction between
intransitivity and inconsistency (incoherence) is analogous to the
distinction between clinical (or methodological) heterogeneity
and statistical heterogeneity in standard pair-wise meta-analysis
(Cipriani 2013).
At a global level, we assessed heterogeneity and inconsistency
(incoherence) of the whole network by decomposing the Q-statistic
into variation of the efect estimates within designs (heterogeneity)
and between designs (inconsistency) (Higgins 2012; Krahn 2013).
A design is each combination of treatments within a study in a
network meta-analysis (e.g. for treatments A, B, and C, possible
designs are A:B, A:C, B:C, and A:B:C). In addition, we used the full
random-efects design-by-treatment interaction model to assess
whether all interventions behave similarly in all comparisons.
We used the R package netmeta for Q decomposition and
for calculation of the full random-efects design-by-treatment
interaction model (netmeta).
At a local level, we assessed diferences between direct and
indirect efect estimates of specific comparisons (incoherence)
using descriptive Z-tests and clinical relevance of the efect
estimates. However, only clinically relevant incoherence based on
diferent clinical conclusions of the 95% CI of direct and indirect
treatment efect estimates with respect to the range of equivalence
was used for interpretation of incoherence.

Investigation of heterogeneity
In cases of statistical heterogeneity (Q-test with P < 0.05, 95% PI
compared to 95% CI) within treatment comparisons, we explored
possible sources (Higgins 2019). We restricted these explorative
analyses to primary and GRADE-relevant secondary outcomes
and to the efect modifier 'dose of the intervention' as potential
sources of heterogeneity. For pair-wise comparisons (drugs of
direct interest versus placebo), we performed subgroup analyses in
RevMan. For the network, we used the R package netmeta to carry
out separate analyses for the subgroups (netmeta).
Diferent treatment regimens—subgroup analysis of doses
Because it is of interest for clinicians and patients to know the
optimal dose of antiemetic drugs with respect to eficacy and
safety, we performed subgroup analyses.
We excluded combinations of drugs from the subgroup analysis
because we cannot be sure whether some combinations can afect
the dose efects. We performed the subgroup analysis of doses in
the network with single drugs only (see 'Sensitivity analysis—Single
drugs only') if the efect estimates remained robust compared to
the primary analysis.
We separated diferent doses of the same drug into low,
recommended, and high doses (Table 1). We restricted splitting of
doses to single drugs of direct interest. The recommended doses or
dose ranges for drugs are based on those reported in the ‘consensus
guidelines for the management of postoperative nausea and
vomiting’ (Gan 2014). For emerging substances, we used doses or
dose ranges based on dose-finding studies (e.g. for amisulpride, see
Kranke 2013; no data are available for fosaprepritant).
We categorized the spectrum of available fixed doses into
low, recommended, and high doses according to the following
algorithm.
•
If a single dose X is recommended (Gan 2014), we defined X as the
‘recommended dose’; ‘low dose’ as < X; ‘high dose’ as > X (lower
and upper limits are defined only if reported in Gan 2014).
•
If a dose range X to Y is recommended (Gan 2014), we defined X
to Y as ‘recommended dose range’; ‘low dose’ as < X; ‘high dose’
as > Y (lower and upper limits are defined only if reported in Gan
2014).
If flexible doses (e.g. mg/kg) were reported, we transformed flexible
doses into fixed doses by multiplying the flexible dose by the mean/
median weight of participants reported in the published study (if
the weight was not reported, we assumed 70 kg).
Drugs without any dose recommendation according to Table 1
(fosaprepitant, scopolamine) and drugs not of direct interest were
included in the analysis. In these cases, all doses of the same drug
were lumped together in a dose category 'NA'.
If there were studies that used drugs of direct interest that were
not attributable to any dose category in Gan 2014 (e.g. using
diferent application routes), we excluded these studies from the
subgroup analysis. Exclusion of these studies was necessary for
subsequent analyses of additive dose efects (see 'Methods for
analysing additive dose efects') because additional categories that
could not assigned to the additive concept may interfere with the
analysis.
We used the R package netmeta to carry out network meta-analyses
with subgroups (netmeta). Network efect estimates were used
for interpretation of subgroup analyses in this review. In addition,
studies were divided into subgroups in pair-wise meta-analyses of
primary and GRADE-relevant secondary outcomes, and these were
reported in the Data and analyses section. We did not report these
pair-wise subgroup analyses in the Efects of interventions section
to reduce the amount of information provided in review text.
We performed this explorative analysis for all primary and for all
secondary outcomes while considering side efects to answer this
specific question about efects of the 'dose of the intervention' on
efect estimates (Higgins 2019).
We summarized the most commonly used dosages, routes, and
time points of administration of single drugs of direct interest for
the primary outcome vomiting and reported this information in the
Efects of interventions section.
Methods for analysing additive dose efects
We used the subgroup analysis of dose with splitting of drugs
into the dose categories low, recommended, and high doses
(see 'Diferent treatment regimens—subgroup analysis dose') as
primary NMA. We performed a second analysis based on the
assumption that the efects of combined categories (e.g. low +
recommended, low + recommended + high, recommended + high)
are additive sums of their individual categories. This assumption,
together with the network structure, leads to a statistical model
that allows decomposing of observed relative efects into single
dose categories and estimating the efects of the dose categories.
The hypothesis of additivity can be tested by comparing estimates
from this model with those from the primary analysis (subgroup
analysis dose) (Mills 2012). We used the function netcomb of the R
package netmeta version 1.0-1 for analysis (netmeta; Rücker 2019).
Sensitivity analysis
We analysed the robustness of the efect estimates by performing
the following sensitivity analyses.
•
Risk of bias: including only trials at low risk of bias in the overall
risk of bias summary (see 'overall risk of bias summary') and
excluding all trials with high or unclear risk of bias in the overall
risk of bias summary.
•
Imbalance in baseline details: Including only trials with a
balanced distribution of baseline details in the study arms and
excluding all studies with imbalance in baseline details in the
study arms.
•
Primary PONV-related outcome: including only trials with
a primary PONV-related outcome and excluding trials that
analysed the outcomes vomiting and nausea not as primary
endpoints.
•
Funding source 'industry': including only trials funded by
industry and excluding all other studies.
•
Funding source 'non-industry': including only trials funded by
non-industry resources and excluding all other studies.
•
Single drugs only: including only study arms investigating single
drugs and excluding study arms investigating combinations
of drugs. This analysis compared the robustness of network
efect estimates of the primary network meta-analysis and the
sensitivity analysis including single drugs only (which is the
basic analysis for the subgroup analysis dose).

Comparability of drug doses within studies: there is a possibility
that some trials compare one drug at the upper limit of its
therapeutic range (e.g. high dose) with another drug at the lower

a dichotomous variable indicating whether the dosages are
comparable (yes = 1) or not (no = 2) and used this information for
sensitivity analysis (Cipriani 2009). Comparable dose categories
were low-low, recommended-recommended, and high-high (for
definitions of dose categories of individual drugs, see Table
1). In the sensitivity analysis, we included only studies that
investigated comparable dose categories of diferent drugs. This
sensitivity analysis was restricted to single drugs only.
•
Adverse event monitoring: we used the information on adverse
event monitoring of studies to test the robustness of efect
estimates for the primary outcomes 'SAE' and 'any AE' by

of bias for adverse event monitoring and excluded high and
unclear risk of bias studies for adverse event monitoring.
We restricted sensitivity analyses to primary outcomes with the

studies', which were relevant for all side efects (GRADE-relevant
secondary outcomes).
We reported efect estimates of the sensitivity analyses of drugs of
direct interest in the section Efects of interventions if the efect
estimates difered from the primary analysis regarding clinical
interpretation of the efect (non-robust efect estimates).
Summary of findings and assessment of the certainty of the
evidence
We presented the main results of the review in ‘Summary of
findings' (SoF) tables including a rating of the certainty of evidence
as suggested for network meta-analysis by Yepes-Nuñez 2019. The
certainty rating was based on the principles of the GRADE Working
Group  and was assessed by an alternative system developed
by Salanti et al (termed CINeMA, Confidence in Network Meta-
Analysis, Salanti 2014).
We created one primary and eleven secondary SoF tables. In the
primary SoF table, single antiemetic drugs of direct interest (see
'Interventions of direct interest') with important beneficial efect
and with high or moderate certainty of evidence for the primary
outcome (vomiting) were presented together with all relevant
substance class-specific adverse events. For the secondary SoF
tables, one table for each outcome (primary outcomes and drug-
class important adverse efects) was created, comparing all single
drugs of direct interest to placebo.
In the SoF tables we presented NMA relative treatment efects,
anticipated absolute efects, ranking of treatments using P scores,
and the certainty of evidence.
The quality of the body of the NMA evidence was assessed by
two independent reviewers (SW, OJ) and reflects within-study
risk of bias (study limitations), across-studies bias (publication
bias), indirectness, imprecision, heterogeneity (variability between
studies within each comparison), and incoherence (variability
between direct and indirect evidence). We have only appraised
the certainty of evidence for relative treatment efects and not for
treatment rankings.
The clinically important size of efect and not the statistical
significance of NMA relative treatment efects was relevant for
assessing the certainty of evidence. We defined for eficacy and
safety outcomes, a range of relative treatment efects around
the line of no efect that do not indicate important clinical
diference between the interventions, which is termed the ‘range of
equivalence’.

Eficacy outcomes (vomiting 0 to 24 hours): a relevant efect is
defined as RR 0.8 (range of equivalence: 0.8 to 1.25)

We GRADEd each network estimate according to the following
criteria (details are described in the Appendix 5):
•
Within-study risk of bias (study limitations)
•
Across-studies bias (publication bias)
•
Indirectness

Imprecision

Heterogeneity

The GRADE assessment resulted in one of four levels of certainty
and these express our confidence in the estimate of efect (Balshem
2011).
•
High certainty: we are very confident that the true efect lies
close to that of the estimate of the efect.
•
Moderate certainty: we are moderately confident in the efect
estimate: the true efect is likely to be close to the estimate of the
efect, but there is a possibility that it is substantially diferent.
•
Low certainty: our confidence in the efect estimate is limited:
the true efect may be substantially diferent from the estimate
of the efect.
•
Very low certainty: we have very little confidence in the efect
estimate: the true efect is likely to be substantially diferent
from the estimate of efect.
Certainty of evidence for efect estimates can vary greatly across
comparisons within a network, and can range from high to very
low certainty. In making inferences regarding the choice of an
intervention recognizing the certainty of each comparison is far
more valuable than ranking eficacy alone (Puhan 2014).

This review is reported based on the PRISMA Extension Statement
for NMA (Hutton 2015) and on the ‘Protocol template for a Cochrane
Intervention review that compares multiple interventions’ from
the Cochrane Comparing Multiple Interventions Methods Group
(Protocol Template 2014).

Comparators
This review compared 21 single interventions of direct interest and
23 additional single interventions to supplement the analysis. All
interventions are listed in Types of interventions. Of 585 included
studies, 541 studies (93%) investigated drugs of direct interest, 19
studies investigated drugs not of direct interest, and 25 studies
investigated both types of interventions.
A total of 384 studies (66%) included an inactive control arm
(placebo or no treatment) in the study design. Active interventions
only were compared in 201 studies (34%). The number of eligible
study arms in included trials ranged between two and 16. In
summary, 310 studies (53%) investigated two groups, 160 studies
(27%) three groups, 77 studies (13%) four groups, 23 studies (4%)
five groups, 11 studies (2%) six groups, two studies (0.3%) seven
groups, and two studies more than seven groups (Apfel 2004-1;
Apfel 2004-2; Beattie 1993).
A total of 423 studies (72%) investigated only single drugs, 31
studies (5%) compared only combinations of drugs, and 131 studies
(23%) compared both single drugs and combinations of drugs.
