The top 10 of the most investigated antiemetic drugs administered
as single prophylaxis for prevention of PONV in this review
were ondansetron (246 studies), dexamethasone (120 studies),
droperidol (97 studies), metoclopramide (76 studies), granisetron
(51 studies), ramosetron (38 studies), palonosetron (35 studies),
tropisetron (32 studies), dolasetron (20 studies), and scopolamine
(18 studies). Thus, the 5-HT3 receptor antagonists are the most
widely studied substance class in this review. Other drugs of
direct interest administered as single interventions were much
less studied, with 10 studies for haloperidol, seven studies for
aprepitant and promethazine, five studies for dimenhydrinate and
methylprednisolone, three studies for fosaprepitant, two studies
for amisulpride, casopitant, and perphenazine, and one study for
rolapitant. No eligible study was found that investigated meclizine
as a single intervention.
Among the combinations of drugs, two-fold combinations were
investigated in 159 studies, three-fold combinations in eight
studies (Apfel 2004-1; Benevides 2013; Bergese 2016; DeOliveira
2011; Gallinger 2007; Liu 2011; Long 2014; Tang 2003), and one
four-fold combination in one study (Hammas 2002). Forty-three
diferent two-fold combinations were used in the included studies.
Four of these two-fold drug combinations were used in 10 or
more studies (54 times: dexamethasone-ondansetron, 20 times:
dexamethasone-granisetron, 15 times: droperidol-ondansetron,
10 times: dexamethasone-metoclopramide). A total of seven
diferent three-fold drug combinations were investigated, of which
dexamethasone-droperidol-ondansetron was used most ofen in
four of eight studies (Apfel 2004-1; Gallinger 2007; Liu 2011; Tang
2003). The other six three-fold combinations were investigated
once each (aprepitant-dexamethasone-ondansetron, aprepitant-
dexamethasone-promethazine, 
dexamethasone-dolasetron-
droperidol, 
dexamethasone-haloperidol-ondansetron,
dexamethasone-metoclopramide-ondansetron, dexamethasone-
ondansetron-promethazine). The only investigated four-fold drug
combination was dexamethasone-droperidol-metoclopramide-
ondansetron.
Details of interventions
We recorded doses, administration time points, and application
routes for all interventions administered as single drugs. We
categorized doses of drugs that are of direct interest into
low, recommended, and high doses according to Table 1. We
categorized time points of administration into before anaesthesia,
at induction of anaesthesia, during surgery, and at end of surgery.
We diferentiated between intravenous, oral, intramuscular, and
other routes of administration (e.g. epidural, intranasal).
Eighty studies (14%) investigated diferent doses of the same
antiemetic drug, 12 studies (2%) diferent administration time
points, and nine studies (2%) diferent routes of application.
5-HT3 receptor antagonists
Dolasetron (20 studies) was administered intravenously or per oral
at doses of 12.5 to 100 mg (recommended to high) and 25 to
200 mg (no dose recommendation available), respectively. Most of
the study arms (56%) investigating intravenous dolasetron used
high doses (> 12.5 mg). Intravenously administered dolasetron was
given at induction of anaesthesia (22%) or at end of surgery (78%).
Oral dolasetron was administered before anaesthesia.
Granisetron (51 studies) was mainly administered via the
intravenous route at doses of 0.1 to 4 mg (low to high). Most of
the study arms (84%) investigating intravenous granisetron used
recommended doses (0.35 to 3 mg). Intravenous granisetron was
given at all diferent time points ranging from before anaesthesia
to end of surgery. Granisetron was administered orally before
anaesthesia at doses of 2 mg in one study (Bhatnagar 2007).
Ondansetron (246 studies) was administered via the intravenous
or oral route at doses of 1 to 16 mg (low to high) and 4 to 16
mg (low to high), respectively. In most of the study arms (71%)
investigating intravenous ondansetron, recommended doses were
used. Low and high doses of intravenous ondansetron were used in
9% and 25% of study arms, respectively. Intravenous ondansetron
was administered most ofen at induction of anaesthesia (69%) and
at end of surgery (26%). Oral ondansetron given before anaesthesia
was investigated in 32% of study arms at low doses, in 47% at
recommended doses, and in 21% at high doses.
Palonosetron (35 studies) was administered only via the
intravenous route at doses of 0.007 to 2.169 mg (low to high). In
most of the study arms, palonosetron was used at recommended
doses (69%), followed by study arms using low doses (21%).
Administration at induction of anaesthesia was used most ofen
(69%), followed by administration at end of surgery (28%).
Ramosetron (38 studies) was administered intravenously or per
oral at doses of 0.1 to 0.45 mg (low to high) and 0.1 mg (no
dose recommendation available), respectively. Most study arms
(89%) investigating intravenous ramosetron used recommended
doses. Administration of intravenous ramosetron at end of surgery
was used most ofen (67%), followed by administration at
induction of anaesthesia (28%). Oral ramosetron (three studies)
was administered before anaesthesia.
Tropisetron (32 studies) was administered intravenously or per
oral at doses of 0.5 to 7.25 mg (low to high) and 5 mg
(no dose recommendation available), respectively. Most study
arms investigating intravenous tropisetron used high doses
(69%), followed by recommended doses (25%). Administration
of intravenous tropisetron at induction of anaesthesia was used
most ofen (75%), followed by administration at end of surgery
(19%). Oral tropisetron (three studies) was administered before
anaesthesia.

Amisulpride (two studies) was administered only via the

intravenous droperidol used recommended doses (57%), followed
by high doses (37%). Intravenous low-dose droperidol was
investigated in 6% of study arms. Intravenous droperidol was given

TIVA in the study design, and we divided participant populations

that anaesthesia was standardized for all participants within the
individual studies (Alia 2015; Backes 2013; Barrow 1994; Gesztesi

Population baseline details
The overall mean age of populations in all included studies in this
review was 42.4 years, and the median age was 42.5 years. Thirty-
four studies (6%) reported a low mean age between 18 and 29
years, and 15 studies (3%) reported a high mean age of more than
60 years. Thirty studies (5%) did not report the mean age of the
study population. Most of the included participants were women
(83%). In 412 studies (70%), included participants were healthy
individuals (American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) 1 and 2).
In 100 studies (17%), participants were eligible with substantial
physical and functional limitations (ASA > 2). In 73 studies (12%),
ASA physical health status was not reported.
We collected study population data on the four risk factors for PONV
according to Apfel (female gender, non-smoker status, history
of PONV or motion sickness, postoperative opioid use). Females
only were included in 292 studies (50%), whereas four studies (<
1%) included only males. In 93 studies (16%), a balanced gender
distribution with 40% to 60% females was reported. Twenty-seven
studies (5%) did not report the gender distribution. A non-smoking
status of 100% in the study population was reported in 55 studies
(9%). Only active smoking participants were included in one study
(Jo 2012). In 399 studies (68%), the smoking status of the study
population was not reported. A history of PONV or motion sickness
in 100% of the study population was reported in five—Altorjay 2011;
Dagtekin 2009; Kim SH 2013; Koivuranta 1999; Pan 2008—and four
studies—Altorjay 2011; Dagtekin 2009; Kim SH 2013; Pan 2008—
respectively. Exclusion of participants with history of PONV or
motion sickness was reported in 100 (17%) and 104 (18%) studies,
respectively. In 266 (45%) and 299 studies (51%), respectively, no
details on participant history of PONV and motion sickness were
reported. In 514 studies (88%), participants received perioperative
opioids. In 15 studies (3%), no perioperative opioids were used.
For 153 studies (26%), data were provided for all four risk factors.
High-risk populations with participants having three and four risk
factors at 100% (inclusion criteria) were studied in five—Altorjay
2011; Dagtekin 2009; Kim SH 2013; NKT102552; Pan 2008—and 31
studies, respectively—a total of 6% of all studies. Two risk factors at
100% (inclusion criteria) were reported in 242 studies (41%).
Study conduct (location, setting, funding)
A total of 298 studies (51%) were conducted in Asia, followed by
Europe with 148 studies (25%) and North America with 96 studies
(16%). Eleven studies (2%) were conducted in South America, nine
studies (2%) in Africa, and seven studies (1%) in Australia/Oceania.
Sixteen studies (3%) were carried out in several countries.
A total of 489 studies (84%) were conducted at a single centre,
and 60 studies (10%) were conducted at multi-centres. The largest
multi-centre study (with 58 study centres) was Morris 1998. In
36 studies (6%), the number of involved studies centres was not
reported.
Inpatient participants were included in 409 studies (70%), and
outpatient participants were included in 103 studies (18%). Twenty-
one studies included both inpatient and outpatient participants,
and 52 studies (9%) did not report this study setting.
A total of 97 studies (17%) have reported that they were funded
by industry, and 104 studies (18%) have reported that they were
funded by non-industrial resources. A majority of studies with a
total of 384 studies (66%) have not declared any details on funding
of the study.
Sample size
The mean sample size of all studies was 167 participants, and the
median sample size was 100, with an interquartile range of 70 to
160 participants. The smallest sample size reported in a study was
20 participants with two study groups (Seki 2005), and the largest
randomized sample size was 5199 participants with 16 study arms
(Apfel 2004-1; Apfel 2004-2). A total of seven studies included more
than 1000 participants (Apfel 2004-1; Fortney 1998; Hechler 2001;
Morris 1998; Pearman 1994; Philip 2000; Scuderi 2001).
Study focus and reported outcomes
The titles of the studies indicated that 516 studies (88%) had a focus
on PONV research. The titles of 69 studies (12%) did suggest a focus
other than PONV research. Most of these studies (33%) investigated
dexamethasone on postoperative recovery.
A total of 309 studies (53%) explicitly specified a primary study
outcome(s) or provided a sample size calculation for one specific
outcome. A total of 86% of these primary outcomes were PONV,
nausea, or vomiting, and 14% were not PONV-related. A total of 276
studies (47%) have not specified which reported outcome was the
primary outcome and did not provide any sample calculation.
A total of 522 studies (89%) investigated relevant eficacy outcomes
for this review. In 327 studies (56%), relevant safety outcomes
were reported. Eighteen studies (3%) did not report numerical
data that can be used in meta-analyses for this review (Aasboe
1998; Altunkaya 2003; Asadollah 2014; Barros 2013; Barrow 1994;
Cubukcu 2007; Derbent 2005; Forrester 2007; Gupta 2011; Judkins
1982; Khanna 1965; Kim WJ 2013; Mohammadi 2007; Ozdamar 2006;
Ploner 1997; Sniadach 1997; Turner 2004; Vale 2011). These studies
provided general statements on relevant safety outcomes.

Excluded studies
We excluded 673 articles (690 records) afer reviewing the full
texts. Reasons for exclusion are listed under Characteristics of
excluded studies. The most common reason for exclusion was a
wrong administration time point of the interventions (afer the
occurrence of PONV, therapeutic not prophylactic intention) with
a total of 136 studies (19%), followed by abstracts with 89 studies
(13), non-clinical study reports (editorials, commentaries, narrative
reviews) with 80 studies (12%), wrong outcomes with 76 studies
(11%), paediatric or mixed populations (adults and children) with
68 studies (10%), regional or sedative anaesthesia with 57 studies
(8%), wrong study design with 48 studies (7%), wrong or no eligible
comparator with 42 studies (6%), diferent baseline anaesthesia
regimens in study arms with 31 studies (5%), wrong intervention
with 29 studies (4%), wrong population with seven studies (1%),
retracted studies (e.g. authored by Fujii) or notes to retracted
studies with six studies (1%), and meta-analysis with four studies
(1%).
Studies awaiting classification
A total of 245 studies (252 records) are awaiting classification. Of
these, 185 studies were identified during the first search in 2017,
with 86 studies reported as full-text journal publications and 99 as
study protocols posted on either ClinicalTrials.gov or WHO ICTRP.
The other 60 studies were identified afer the first search or during
the search update in 2020. Thirty-nine of these 60 studies will be
fully included in the next review update, and 21 studies are awaiting
classification due to missing study information. Details on studies
awaiting classification are listed in the Characteristics of studies
awaiting classification tables.
Of the 86 studies identified in the first search and reported as
journal publications, no full text was available for 29 studies.
Amongst the missing information of studies with full text were
lack of population age (19 studies), details on the anaesthesia
regimen (11 studies), randomization details (eight studies), study
design (eight studies), outcome details (six studies), and time
point of drug administration (one study). Two studies from an
author for whom several publications were currently retracted or
listed in the retraction watch database are awaiting classification
until resolution of concerns (Schietroma 2010; Schietroma 2013).
Two other studies seem to share identical study arms without
co-referencing each other (Isazadehfar 2016; Isazadehfar 2017).
Requests for missing information were sent to all authors who
reported contact email addresses in the journal publication.
Requests regarding 18 studies remained unanswered.
Of the 99 study protocols retrieved in the first search, three
protocols posted results on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT00231777;
NCT01149616; NCT01612702). Due to missing contact email
addresses, missing information on the anaesthesia regimen or the
time point of administration could not be clarified. The status of
25 studies was 'not yet recruiting' or 'recruitment' at the time
of the search. The status of 71 studies was 'closed', 'completed',
'terminated', or 'unknown', and none of the protocols could be
allocated to one of the included or excluded studies of the current
review. Missing information for individual studies that are allocated
to awaiting classification is provided under Characteristics of
studies awaiting classification.
Risk of bias in included studies
The risk of bias of each included study was rated, and details
on judgements are described in the Characteristics of included
studies section. All judgements about each risk of bias item
for each included study are graphically presented in Figure
5 (higher-resolution image is available online: Supplementary
File_Summary of Risk of bias). Judgements about each risk of
bias item presented as percentages across all included studies
are graphically presented in Figure 6. About half of all studies
were rated as low risk of bias for random sequence generation
(48%), blinding of participants and personnel (46%), and blinding
of outcome assessors (61%). Incomplete reporting of outcome data
was a minor problem in this review, as 90% of studies have been
assessed as having low risk of attrition bias. Major problems were
unclear risk of selection bias due to insuficient information on
allocation concealment and unclear risk of reporting bias due to
lack of registered study protocols. Only 12% of all studies were
assessed as having low risk of allocation concealment, and only
2% of all studies were assessed as having low risk of selective
outcome reporting. The item 'other bias' captures the risk of
baseline imbalance, and 12% of all studies were assessed as having
low risk due to reporting on all relevant population details and
prognostic variables, without any imbalance in these data.

Allocation
Random sequence generation
A total of 282 studies (48%) have reported adequate methods for
sequence generation such as random number tables or computer-
generated random numbers. These 282 studies were assessed as
having low risk of bias. One randomized study was assessed as
having high risk of selection bias according to a statement on the
potential threat due to selection bias reported in the results section
without further description of the study protocol (NCT00888329).
All of the other 302 studies (52%) have not reported suficient
information on the method used for random sequence generation.
Most ofen, these studies have stated only that the study was
randomized without describing the method; therefore we assessed
them as having unclear risk of bias.
Allocation concealment
Sixty-nine studies (12%) were judged to have low risk of bias
because allocation concealment was achieved by using central
allocation or sequentially numbered opaque sealed envelopes
(SNOSE). Two studies were assessed as having high risk of bias
(NCT00888329; Olajumoke 2013). NCT00888329 reported the risk
of selection bias as a limitation in the study protocol. Olajumoke
2013 was judged as having high risk because there was a high
possibility that assignments could be foreseen by using an open
random allocation schedule. A total of 514 studies (88%) did not
describe any method used for allocation concealment, or it was not
clear from the description whether SNOSE was correctly applied to
cover allocation. These studies were assessed as having unclear risk
of bias.
Blinding
Blinding of participants and personnel
In 271 studies (46%), it was reported that participants and
personnel were blinded. Sixty-seven studies (12%) had an
unblinded study design. Most ofen, anaesthesiologists responsible
for intraoperative management were not blinded to the treatment.
In 247 studies (42%), there was no or insuficient information
on blinding of participants or personnel, and statements such as
'blinded study' or 'double-blind study' were used. These studies
were assessed as having unclear risk of bias.
Blinding of outcome assessment
In 355 studies (61%), it was reported that outcome assessors were
blinded. Four studies (< 1%) had an unblinded study design (Dsouza
2011; Laha 2013; Lee WS 2015; Wattwil 2003). In 226 studies (39%),
there was no or insuficient information on blinding of outcome
assessors, and statements such as 'blinded study' or 'double-blind
study' were used. These studies were assessed as having unclear
risk of bias.
Incomplete outcome data
A total of 528 studies (90%) were judged as having low risk of
attrition bias, 27 studies (5%) high risk, and 30 studies (5%) unclear
risk.
Selective reporting
The risk of selective outcome reporting bias can be reliably
assessed only if a study protocol was prospectively registered. A
total of 510 studies (87%) have not published a study protocol
available on the ClinicalTrials.gov or WHO ICTRP database. All of
these studies were at unclear risk of reporting bias. Of the other 75
studies with registered study protocols, 58 studies have referenced
the study protocol in the journal publication, six studies without
a full-text journal publication have reported study results in the
study protocol or the study report (NCT00888329; NKO101287;
NKT102245; NKT102260; NKT102552; PALO-04-07), and 11 studies
have not referenced their registered study protocols in the
published journal report, and vice versa (Agarkar 2015; Alghanem
2010; Bang 2017; Blitz 2012; Choi 2016; Jung 2013; Kakuta 2011;
Kim SH 2013; Kizilcik 2017; Ryoo 2015; Sanchez Rodriguez 2010).
The 11 corresponding study protocols were retrieved in our search
of the ClinicalTrials.gov or WHO ICTRP database, and we could
allocate the protocols to the published journal reports based on
corresponding study details.
Of the 75 studies (13%) with registered study protocols, 27 studies
(5% of all 585 studies) were prospectively registered, 47 (8%) were
retrospectively registered, and one could not be assessed due to
diferent study dates in the protocol and in the report (Kim 2015).
Of the 27 studies with prospectively registered protocols, 11 studies
(2% of all 585 studies) were assessed as having low risk of selective
outcme reporting bias (Altorjay 2011; Bjerregaard 2018; Gan 2011;
Kranke 2012; Kranke 2013; NKO101287; NKT102245; NKT102552;
PALO-04-07; Tarantino 2015; Tolver 2012), 10 studies (2%) were
assessed as having high risk of selective outcome reporting bias
(DeOliveira 2011; Fahlenkamp 2016; Green 2012; Hu 2017; Kim
SH 2013; Sinha 2014; Soga 2015; Vallejo 2012; Yang 2017; Zhou
2012), and six studies were assessed as having unclear risk of
selective outcome reporting bias (Corcoran 2017; Dewinter 2016;
Kakuta 2011; Kakuta 2015; Segelman 2016; Tsutsumi 2014). All
retrospectively registered studies were assessed as having unclear
risk of reporting bias.
Other potential sources of bias
A total of 71 studies (12%) have had no baseline imbalance in
population characteristics or risk factors for PONV between study
arms and were judged as having low risk of other bias. Ninety-seven
studies (17%) showed an imbalance and were judged as having
high risk of other bias. In 417 studies (71%), information on relevant
population characteristics or risk factors for PONV was missing, and
we judged these studies as having unclear risk of other bias.
Assessment of adverse events monitoring
Sixty-one studies (10%) reported data on the outcome 'any AE'. We
assessed the ways of definition and monitoring of any AE (Table
2). Eleven studies were judged as having low risk of bias because

of bias because substance class-specific adverse events were not
included or reported under the composite outcome AE, and there
were no details on monitoring of AEs reported, or AEs were not
actively monitored. Twenty-three studies provided no details on
monitoring of AEs reported nor on all relevant substance class-

Subgroup analysis of vomiting: dose efects
To account for the treatment efect modifier dose, we performed a
subgroup network meta-analysis splitting drugs into the categories
low, recommended, and high doses according to Table 1. We
restricted splitting of doses to single drugs.
First, we conducted a network meta-analysis including single
drugs only (and excluding combination treatments) with 230
RCTs and 29 treatments including placebo. The network was well
connected, and efect estimates as well as the ranking order of
drugs with placebo as comparator were comparable to the primary
analysis, including combination prophylaxis. The estimated value
of between-study variance for the network meta-analysis of single
drugs for vomiting was 0.061 (tau2) (I2 = 48.3%).
Second, we conducted the subgroup analysis on dose for the
network of single drugs only. We split the following drugs into dose
categories: amisulpride, aprepitant, dexamethasone, dolasetron,
droperidol, granisetron, haloperidol, ondansetron, palonosetron,
promethazine, ramosetron, rolapitant, and tropisetron. For
casopitant, dimenhydrinate, and metoclopramide, only one dose
category (low, recommended, or high) was available for the
subgroup analysis. Drugs without any dose recommendation
according to Table 1 (fosaprepitant, scopolamine) and drugs
not of direct interest (alizapride, betamethasone, buspirone,
CP-122,721, cyclizine, dixyrazine, domperidone, penehyclidine,
prednisolone, prochlorperazine) were included in the analysis and
were lumped together, irrespective of the doses being analysed,
in a category labelled 'NA'. We excluded six studies from the
subgroup analysis because they were not attributable to one of the
three dose categories (Eberhart 2006; Heidari 2015b; Huseyinoglu
2016; Jakobsson 1999; Phillips 1993; Verhasselt 1988). We split
the subgroup network meta-analysis with 224 studies and 29
treatments including placebo into 50 nodes with dose categories,
and this is presented in the online repository. In ranking of drugs
according to eficacy with placebo as the comparator for higher
or recommended doses of drugs ranked higher than lower doses,
however, most of the 95% CIs were overlapping between diferent
dose categories of the same drug. For dexamethasone, droperidol,
granisetron, ondansetron, rolapitant, and tropisetron, the 95%
CIs of the low doses showed uncertain benefit in contrast to
recommended and/or high doses of the same drug.
We have summarized the most commonly used dosages, routes,
and time points of administration of single drugs of direct interest
for the primary outcome vomiting in Table 3.
Additivity of dose categories (vomiting)
A network meta-analysis with the assumption of additivity of dose
categories revealed similar results as the standard network meta-
analysis model when point estimates and 95% CIs were compared,
suggesting additive dose efects. However, the Q-statistic of the
diference between standard and additive network meta-analyses
for vomiting suggests that the standard model explained the data
better than the additive model (P = 0.03). This may be due to the fact
that, for all drugs, the categories high and recommended for the
same drug showed similar efect estimates, which generally were
more efective than the corresponding low dose categories.

categories). The analysis included only studies investigating
drugs of direct interest for which dose recommendations were
described and were assigned to one of the dose categories
according to Table 1. The network of this sensitivity analysis
consisted of 15 treatments including placebo. Rolapitant and

Additive efects of combinations of treatments (vomiting)
We tested the hypothesis of additivity of the components in
combination prophylaxis by comparing the primary standard
analysis (k = 282) with a second analysis, which assumes that
the efects of combined treatments are additive sums of their
components. This assumption is very strong and general, as the
analysis assumes additive efects for all components included in
the analysis. The Q-statistic of the diference between standard
and additive network meta-analyses for vomiting suggests that
the standard model explained the data better than the additive
model (P = 0.006). On the level of individual comparisons, the
additive model shrunk the efects compared to the standard

may indicate negative interaction of the components. For all
other combinations of treatments, especially the combinations
used most frequently (dexamethasone-ondansetron, droperidol-

additive models were comparable, suggesting additive efects of
the single components.

Certainty of evidence: vomiting
The certainty of evidence of treatment estimates for vomiting
evaluated with CINeMA is summarized in the 'Summary of findings'

of evidence for ondansetron (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.60) and
granisetron (RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.54), which also reduce
vomiting compared to placebo, was also rated as high. However,
high certainty of evidence applies to recommended and high
doses of ondansetron and granisetron because low doses showed
no clinically important benefit. Tropisetron (RR 0.52, 95% CI
0.43 to 0.63) and dolasetron (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.74)
may reduce vomiting compared to placebo, with low-certainty
evidence for tropisetron (serious concerns for study limitation)
and dolasetron (study limitation, heterogeneity-incoherence). Low
certainty of evidence for tropisetron is restricted to recommended
and high doses. Palonosetron (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.80) may
reduce vomiting, for which the certainty of evidence is low (study
limitation, imprecision).
For relevant D2 receptor antagonists (compared to placebo), the
certainty of evidence of network efect estimates for vomiting 0 to
24 hours ranged from very low to moderate (Summary of findings
2). Droperidol (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.69) probably reduces
vomiting, with moderate-certainty evidence (publication bias-
heterogeneity). However, moderate certainty of evidence applies
to recommended and high doses of droperidol. Amisulpride (RR
0.71, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.09), with direct evidence only, probably
reduces vomiting, with moderate-certainty evidence (imprecision-
heterogeneity). Haloperidol (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.87)
may reduce vomiting, with low-certainty evidence (imprecision,

evidence (study limitation, imprecision, incoherence). No studies
reporting vomiting were available for perphenazine.
For relevant NK1 receptor antagonists (compared to placebo), the
certainty of evidence of network efect estimates for vomiting 0 to
24 hours ranged from very low to high (Summary of findings 2).
Fosaprepitant (RR 0.06, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.21), casopitant (RR 0.16,

SAEs within seven days postoperatively
Pairwise meta-analyses (single drugs of direct interest versus placebo)
of SAEs
Pairwise meta-analyses for SAEs comparing single drugs of
direct interest versus placebo are presented in the Data and
analyses section and were available for amisulpride (Analysis
1.2), dexamethasone (Analysis 3.2), dolasetron (Analysis 5.2),
droperidol (Analysis 6.2), granisetron (Analysis 7.2), ondansetron
(Analysis 11.2), palonosetron (Analysis 12.2), ramosetron (Analysis
15.2), scopolamine (Analysis 17.2), and tropisetron (Analysis 18.2).
Studies or study arms were separated according to dose categories
of single drugs (low, recommended, high, NA).
Primary analysis of SAEs: network meta-analysis with all single drugs
and drug combinations
Raw data of individual studies and all analyses for the outcome
SAEs are available in an online repository (Supplementary Files-2-
SAE ; including direct and indirect efect estimates to the primary
NMA, network graphs, and forest plots to all sensitivity and subgroup
analyses, explorative analyses of reporting bias, and funnel plots).
Twenty-nine studies with 10,886 participants were eligible for the
network meta-analysis of SAEs. Twelve studies (41%) have reported
zero events in all study arms. One study was not connected
to the network and was excluded from the following analysis:
Papadimitriou 2001; comparison: metoclopramide-tropisetron
versus metoclopramide. The network of the remaining 28 studies
with 52 pair-wise comparisons due to multi-arm studies included
22 treatments (nodes), of which placebo (k = 26) and ondansetron
(k = 14) were the most frequent comparators (Figure 10). Of
the 22 treatments, eight were two-fold drug combinations, 13
were single drugs, and one was placebo or no treatment. The
most common comparisons with three studies each were between
ondansetron versus placebo, dexamethasone versus placebo,
dolasetron versus placebo, palonosetron versus placebo, and
casopitant-ondansetron versus ondansetron. Of all single drugs
of direct interest included in the network of SAEs, amisulpride,
dolasetron, palonosetron, and scopolamine were connected only
to placebo, and aprepitant was connected only to ondansetron.

Sensitivity analyses of SAEs
Sensitivity analyses included all single drugs and drug
combinations, but results are described only for single drugs of
direct interest compared to placebo.
Sensitivity analysis of SAEs: risk of bias
Three (11%) of 28 studies were rated as having high risk of
overall bias, 14 (50%) as unclear, and 11 (39%) as low. The
sensitivity network meta-analysis including only studies at low risk
of bias revealed a poorly connected network, with 11 treatments
and 11 studies. Three treatments were two-fold combinations
of antiemetic drugs, seven treatments were single drugs, and
one was placebo or no treatment. Of the single drugs of direct
interest, granisetron, tropisetron, ramosetron, dolasetron, and
scopolamine were not included in the sensitivity network meta-
analysis due to lack of studies with low risk of bias. Efect
estimates of five single drugs (aprepitant, ondansetron, casopitant,
dexamethasone, palonosetron) compared to placebo in this
sensitivity analysis were not robust when compared to the primary
network meta-analysis. Aprepitant, ondansetron, and casopitant
with RR 0.23 (95% CI 0.00 to 11.55), RR 0.26 (95% CI 0.01 to 13.12),
and RR 0.59 (95% CI 0.01 to 32.74), respectively, showed benefit
associated with uncertainty. Dexamethasone and palonosetron
showed no or minimal efects, with RR 1.00 (95% CI 0.02 to 49.75)
and RR 1.00 (95% CI 0.02 to 49.43), respectively—both associated
with uncertainty. The estimated value of between-study variance
for the sensitivity network meta-analysis of SAEs was 0 (tau2) (I2 =
0%).
Sensitivity analysis of SAEs: risk of bias for monitoring and reporting
of SAEs
In a sensitivity network meta-analysis for monitoring and reporting
of SAEs, we included only studies that have defined SAEs
in the study report according to an accepted international
classification system. Only five (18%) of 28 studies were assessed
as having low risk of bias for monitoring and reporting of SAEs.
The five studies were not connected. Two studies compared
either granisetron—Hanaoka 2004—or dexamethasone—Tarantino
2015—to placebo, and three studies from GlaxoSmithKline
compared casopitant-ondansetron or casopitant to ondansetron
(NKT102245; NKT102260; NKT102552). Compared to the primary
analysis, the treatment efect for dexamethasone versus placebo
was not robust and showed no or minimal efect associated with
uncertainty (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.02 to 49.75). Casopitant showed
harm associated with uncertainty compared to ondansetron (RR
2.25, 95% CI 0.91 to 5.58).
Sensitivity analysis of SAEs: imbalance in baseline details and/or risk
factors for PONV in study participants
We assessed studies with an imbalance in baseline details and/
or risk factors for PONV between the study arms as having
high risk of other bias. For SAEs, three (11%) of 28 studies
were rated as high risk of other bias, 18 (64%) as unclear,
and seven (25%) as low. The seven studies with low risk of
other bias were not connected in one network. Four of these
studies with 10 treatments including placebo as comparator
were connected in one sub-network. Three other studies from
GlaxoSmithKline with ondansetron as comparator were included
in the other sub-network (NKT102245; NKT102260; NKT102552).
Of the single drugs, dolasetron, aprepitant, scopolamine, and
amisulpride were not included in the sensitivity network meta-
analysis due to lack of studies with low risk of bias. Compared
to the primary analysis, treatment efects for palonosetron,
granisetron, droperidol, dexamethasone, all compared to placebo,
were not robust and showed no or minimal efect associated with
uncertainty.
Sensitivity analysis of SAEs: studies with PONV-related primary
outcome(s)
Twenty-two (79%) of 28 studies have defined a PONV-related
primary outcome in their published study report. The network
of this sensitivity analysis consisted of 18 treatments including
placebo (six combination and 11 single drug treatments). Of the
single drugs, ramosetron and scopolamine were not included in
the sensitivity network meta-analysis due to lack of studies with
low risk of bias. The relative treatment efects of all single drugs
compared to placebo were comparable to the primary analysis,
with RRs ranging between 0.31 (95% CI 0.10 to 1.00) for dolasetron
and 4.07 (95% CI 0.60 to 27.64) for casopitant. The estimated
value of between-study variance for this sensitivity network meta-
analysis of SAE was 0 (tau2) (I2 = 0%).

studies funded by non-industrial resources consisted of six studies
with three combinations, six single drugs, and placebo. Compared

Reporting bias (SAE)
None of the direct pair-wise comparisons included 10 or more
studies. Therefore, analyses investigating reporting or publication
bias were not performed.
Subgroup analysis of SAEs: dose efects
The treatment efect modifier dose was investigated in a subgroup
network meta-analysis splitting drugs into the categories low,
recommended, and high doses according to Table 1. Splitting of
doses was restricted to single drugs.
First, a network meta-analysis including single drugs only (and
excluding combination treatments) with 22 studies and 14
treatments including placebo was conducted. Network geometry,
efect estimates, and the ranking order of drugs with placebo as
comparator were comparable to the primary analysis, including
combination prophylaxis. The estimated value of between-study
variance for the network meta-analysis of single drugs for SAEs was
0 (tau2) (I2 = 0%).
Second, the subgroup analysis of dose was conducted for the
network of single drugs only. The following drugs were split into
dose categories: amisulpride, aprepitant, dolasetron, ondansetron,
palonosetron, and ramosetron. For casopitant, dexamethasone,
droperidol, granisetron, and tropisetron, only one dose category
was available for subgroup analysis. Drugs without any dose
recommendation according to Table 1 (scopolamine) and drugs not
of direct interest (olanzapine) were included in the analysis and
were lumped together, irrespective of the doses being analysed,
in the category 'NA'. Three studies—Diemunsch 1998; Eberhart
2006; Warriner 1997—and one arm of Lee 2008a (0.1 mg oral
ramosetron) were excluded from the subgroup analysis because
they were not associated with one of the three dose categories.
The network was poorly connected, with 19 studies and 14
treatments split into 21 nodes with dose categories. Ranking of
drugs according to safety with placebo as comparator is presented
in the online repository. All available dose categories for dolasetron
and palonosetron compared to placebo showed benefit associated
with uncertainty. For aprepitant, all dose categories compared to
placebo showed harm associated with uncertainty. Amisulpride
used as recommended or low doses showed benefit, high doses
showed harm, and all treatment efects were associated with
uncertainty. Low doses of ramosetron showed no or minimal
efect and recommended doses showed harm, and both treatment
efects were associated with uncertainty. Recommended doses
of ondansetron showed harm, high doses showed benefit, and
both treatment efects were associated with high uncertainty.
Recommended doses of casopitant (RR 42.47, 95% CI 1.98 to
910.14) showed important harm. However, evidence for these
results was restricted to only one study directly comparing
recommended doses of casopitant and ondansetron. Casopitant
was not otherwise connected in the network.

A network meta-analysis with the assumption of additivity of the

additive models (P = 0.34), suggesting additive dose efects. The
analysis was based on a few studies that currently make reliable
statements on additive efects of drug doses impossible.

connected, consisting of 11 treatments including placebo, which

high uncertainty. Dexamethasone showed no or minimal efect,

Sensitivity analyses of any AE
Sensitivity analyses included all single drugs and drug
combinations, but results are described only for single drugs of
direct interest compared to placebo.
Sensitivity analysis of any AE: risk of bias
Nine (15%) of 61 studies were rated as having high risk of overall
bias, 31 (51%) as unclear, and 21 (34%) as low. The sensitivity
network meta-analysis including only studies at low risk of bias
revealed a poorly connected network, including 18 treatments.
Six treatments were two-fold combinations of antiemetic drugs,
11 were single drugs, and one was placebo. Of the single
drugs of direct interest included in the primary network meta-
analysis of any AE, dolasetron, palonosetron, dimenhydrinate, and
scopolamine were not included in the sensitivity network meta-
analysis due to lack of studies with low risk of bias. Of the 11
single drugs, four drugs showed important benefit compared to
placebo (aprepitant, casopitant, ondansetron, metoclopramide),
with RRs ranging between 0.50 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.82) for aprepitant
and 0.54 (95% CI 0.33 to 0.89) for metoclopramide. None of
the four drugs showed important benefit compared to placebo
in the primary network meta-analysis. Proof of data revealed
one small outlier study comparing ondansetron versus placebo
with extreme positive efects for ondansetron (Koyuncu 2017).
Excluding Koyuncu 2017 and redoing the sensitivity analysis for
risk of bias revealed that none of the treatments maintained
important benefit compared to placebo. Thus, favourable efects
for aprepitant, casopitant, ondansetron, and metoclopramide in
the first sensitivity analysis for risk of bias may be due to strong
efects reported by Koyuncu 2017.
Comparison of treatment efects of the sensitivity analysis for
risk of bias without Koyuncu 2017, and the primary network
meta-analysis for any AE revealed seven drugs compared
to placebo with non-robust treatment efects (ramosetron,
aprepitant, casopitant, droperidol, dexamethasone, ondansetron,
metoclopramide). Ramosetron compared to placebo with RR 0.79
(95% CI 0.26 to 2.41) showed benefit with uncertainty. Aprepitant
and casopitant compared to placebo, with RR 1.00 (95% CI 0.48 to
2.09) and RR 1.02 (95% CI 0.47 to 2.19), respectively, showed no or
minimal efect associated with uncertainty. Droperidol compared
to placebo, with RR 1.32 (95% CI 0.64 to 2.72), showed harm
associated with uncertainty. For dexamethasone, ondansetron,
and metoclopramide, the uncertainty of efect estimates was
increased further in the sensitivity analysis compared to the
primary network meta-analysis. The estimated value of between-
study variance for the sensitivity network meta-analysis of any AE
was 0 (tau2) (I2 = 0%).
Sensitivity analysis of any AE: risk of bias for monitoring and reporting
of any AE
In a sensitivity network meta-analysis for monitoring and reporting
of any AE, we included only studies that were assessed as
low risk of bias with respect to monitoring and reporting
for any AE. We assessed 11 (18%) of 61 studies as having
low risk of bias for monitoring and reporting of any AE. The
network including only studies at low risk of bias was poorly
connected, with two sub-networks that were connected only via
the route ondansetron to placebo. Of the single drugs of direct
interest, dolasetron, droperidol, metoclopramide, palonosetron,
amisulpride, tropisetron, and dimenhydrinate were not included
in the sensitivity network meta-analysis due to lack of studies
assessed as low risk. Treatment efects of three drugs compared
to placebo were not robust in this sensitivity analysis (aprepitant,
casopitant, ramosetron). Aprepitant (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.16)
and casopitant (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.29) showed no or minimal
efect on any AE associated with uncertainty. Ramosetron with RR
1.31 (95% CI 0.73 to 2.38) showed harm associated with uncertainty.
The estimated value of between-study variance for the sensitivity
network meta-analysis of any AE was 0 (tau2) (I2 = 0%).
Sensitivity analysis of any AE: imbalance in baseline details and/or risk
factors for PONV in study participants
We assessed studies with an imbalance in baseline details and/
or risk factors for PONV between the study arms as having high
risk of other bias. For any AE, five (8%) of 61 studies were rated
as having high risk of other bias, 48 (77%) as unclear, and eight
(13%) as low. One study was not connected to the network (Chen
2006; comparison: dexamethasone versus placebo). The remaining
seven studies with low risk of other bias with six treatments were
poorly connected in one network in which placebo was not used as
a comparator. We could not perform a network meta-analysis with
placebo as reference compound.
Sensitivity analysis of any AE: studies with PONV-related primary
outcome(s)
Thirty-four (56%) of 61 studies have defined a PONV-related
primary outcome in their published study report. The network
of this sensitivity analysis consisted of 21 treatments including
placebo with 11 single drug treatments. Of the single drugs of
direct interest, dolasetron, scopolamine, and dimenhydrinate were
not included in this network due to lack of studies reporting a
PONV-related primary outcome. Treatment efects of four drugs
compared to placebo were not robust in this sensitivity analysis
(ramosetron, droperidol, aprepitant, casopitant). Ramosetron with
RR 0.74 (95% CI 0.32 to 1.73) showed benefit associated with
uncertainty. Droperidol (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.02), aprepitant
(RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.07), and casopitant (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.79
to 1.14) showed no or minimal efect on any AE associated with
uncertainty. The estimated value of between-study variance for the
sensitivity network meta-analysis of any AE was 0 (tau2) (I2 = 0%).

Reporting bias (any AE)
The only pair-wise comparison including 10 or more studies was
ondansetron versus placebo, for which small-study efects such
as reporting or publication bias were investigated. Results of
the funnel plot, the arcsine test for funnel plot asymmetry, and
the trim and fill sensitivity analysis are presented in the online
repository. According to the explorative analyses, we did not
suspect publication bias for ondansetron versus placebo (P = 0.19).

The treatment efect modifier dose was investigated in a subgroup

excluding combination treatments) with 48 studies and 16
treatments including placebo was conducted. Network geometry,
efect estimates, and the ranking order of drugs with placebo as
comparator were comparable to the primary analysis, including
combination prophylaxis. The estimated value of between-study
variance for the network meta-analysis of single drugs for any AE
was 0 (tau2) (I2 = 0%).

Additivity of dose categories (any AE)
A network meta-analysis with the assumption of additivity of dose
categories revealed no diferences between standard and additive
models (P = 0.96), suggesting additive dose efects.
Sensitivity analysis of any AE: comparability of doses
In 31 (51%) of 61 studies investigating single drugs, comparable

categories). The analysis included only studies investigating
drugs of direct interest for which dose recommendations were

according to Table 1. The network of this sensitivity analysis
was poorly connected, consisting of 12 treatments including
placebo, which limited available evidence. Of single drugs of
direct interest included in the primary network meta-analysis,
aprepitant, dimenhydrinate, and scopolamine were not included
in the sensitivity analysis due to lack of studies with comparable

compared to placebo were not robust in the sensitivity analysis.

uncertainty. The estimated value of between-study variance for this
sensitivity network meta-analysis of any AE was 0.0069 (tau2) (I2 =

Additive efects of combinations of treatments (any AE)
We tested the hypothesis of additivity of the components in
combination prophylaxis by comparing the primary standard
network meta-analysis (k = 61) with a second analysis, which
assumes that the efects of combined treatments are additive sums
of their components. Standard and additive models were diferent
(P < 0.0001), suggesting no additive efects of components.

Reporting bias (complete response)
Three direct pair-wise comparisons included 10 or more studies
for which small-study efects such as reporting or publication bias
were investigated: dexamethasone, droperidol, and ondansetron,
all compared to placebo. Results of the funnel plots, the arcsine
test for funnel plot asymmetry, and the trim and fill sensitivity
analysis are presented in the online repository. According to
the explorative analyses, we suspected publication bias for the
comparisons droperidol versus placebo (P = 0.10) and ondansetron
versus placebo (P = 0.01). The contour-enhanced funnel plots
also suggested asymmetry for dexamethasone versus placebo.
However, we did not suspect relevant publication bias for this
comparison because trim and fill sensitivity analysis did not change
the conclusion with respect to the range of equivalence. Asymmetry
may have been caused by other factors such as heterogeneity.
D I S C U S S I O N
Summary of main results
This systematic review with network meta-analyses investigated
the eficacy and safety of drugs for prevention of postoperative
nausea and vomiting (PONV) with focus on postoperative vomiting
in adults afer general anaesthesia. It included 585 randomized
controlled trials (RCTs) with 97,516 participants. A total of 44 single
antiemetic drugs belonging to six diferent substance classes (5-
HT3 receptor antagonists, D2 receptor antagonists, NK1 receptor
antagonists, corticosteroids, antihistamines, and anticholinergics)
and 51 drug combinations were investigated. An overview of the
direction and magnitude of efects along with the certainty of
evidence for all GRADE-relevant outcomes and all single drugs of
direct interest, according to Gan 2014, compared to placebo is
summarized in Figure 7.
Primary outcomes
The network meta-analysis (NMA) of the primary eficacy
outcome ‘vomiting within 24 hours postoperatively’ included 282
RCTs, 50,812 participants, and 65 interventions. The certainty
of evidence for single drugs of direct interest compared to
placebo ranged from very low to high. High-certainty evidence
showed that five drugs (aprepitant, ramosetron, granisetron,
dexamethasone, and ondansetron) reduced vomiting, and
moderate-certainty evidence indicated that another two single
drugs (fosaprepitant and droperidol) probably reduced vomiting
compared to placebo (Summary of findings 1; Summary of
findings 2). These are the seven most reliable and most efective
drugs identified in this review for ‘vomiting within 24 hours
postoperatively’. All other single drugs of direct interest involved
evidence of very low to low certainty (casopitant, tropisetron,
and dolasetron), or they were less efective (amisulpride

droperidol, palonosetron, amisulpride, and metoclopramide. Drug
combinations were generally more efective than most of the
single drugs. However, treatment efects of the top three ranked

the baseline risk for serious adverse events (SAEs) with placebo

dolasetron, and palonosetron) were investigated in large RCTs
(> 500 participants/treatment). Thus, the chance to detect rare
SAEs was highest for aprepitant, dolasetron, and palonosetron.
The certainty of evidence for single drugs of direct interest
compared to placebo ranged from very low to low (Summary
of findings 1; Summary of findings 3). In terms of treatment
efects, none of the active treatments showed important harm
or benefit compared to placebo, and all were associated with
uncertainty. In the ranking of treatments with placebo as
comparator, single drugs of direct interest in increasing order
according to the risk of SAEs were dolasetron, tropisetron,

The NMA of the primary safety outcome ‘number of participants
with any AE [adverse event] within seven days postoperatively’
included 61 RCTs, 19,423 participants, and 27 interventions. The
certainty of evidence for single drugs of direct interest compared to
placebo ranged from very low to moderate (Summary of findings
1; Summary of findings 4). Moderate-certainty evidence shows that
granisetron and amisulpride probably had no or little efect on
any AE compared to placebo. Two of the 14 single drugs of direct
interest, namely, dimenhydrinate and scopolamine, have low-
certainty evidence and may increase the number of participants
with any AE compared to placebo. None of the other single drugs
of direct interest showed important harm. All showed benefit or
no efect, but all were associated with only low- or very low-
certainty evidence. In the ranking of treatments with placebo as
comparator, single drugs of direct interest in increasing order
according to the risk of any AE were dexamethasone, aprepitant,
dolasetron, casopitant, droperidol, granisetron, metoclopramide,
ondansetron, palonosetron, ramosetron, amisulpride, tropisetron,
scopolamine, and dimenhydrinate. Of all drug combinations, only
ondansetron-scopolamine showed important benefit for any AE
compared to placebo. No combinations showed important harm.
However, caution is advised, as we have not assessed the certainty
of evidence for any of the drug combinations. Treatment efects of
diferent doses of single drugs did not difer in a clinically relevant
manner and were associated with uncertainty. However, in the
ranking of treatments, high and recommended doses generally
ranked higher than lower doses of the individual drugs in terms
of favourable efects on any AE. Thus, contrary to the intuitive
assumption that lower doses of drugs produce fewer side efects
than higher doses, the opposite seems to be the case here. These
findings could be explained by the fact that prevention of PONV
generally lowers the risk of other adverse efects (Kranke 2018).
Some molecules directly prevent adverse efects, such as headache
when droperidol is used, or act as co-analgesics (e.g. valid for
dexamethasone).

Other secondary outcomes
We have investigated five other secondary outcomes, including
mortality within seven days, along with the eficacy outcomes of
early and late vomiting, nausea, and complete response within 24
hours. We have not assessed the certainty of evidence for drugs
included in the NMAs of these outcomes.
Mortality was reported in only 17 RCTs including 6840 participants.
Only one participant with ondansetron died during the study
period, and study authors reported that the participant´s death
was not drug-related.
The eficacy profile of the seven most efective and most
reliable single drugs for the primary outcome 'vomiting within
24 hours' (fosaprepitant, aprepitant, ramosetron, granisetron,
dexamethasone, ondansetron, and droperidol) showed a slightly
diferent eficacy profile for other eficacy outcomes such as
vomiting (early and late), nausea, and complete response
compared to the primary outcome. For early vomiting, the
benefit of aprepitant was associated with uncertainty, and the
treatment efect of droperidol was slightly better for vomiting
within 24 hours, which was comparable to the other 5-
HT3 receptor antagonists. Treatment efects of fosaprepitant,
granisetron, ramosetron, ondansetron, and dexamethasone were
comparable for early vomiting and vomiting within 24 hours. For
late vomiting, no studies investigated fosaprepitant. Aprepitant
was the most efective drug for late vomiting. Aprepitant,
granisetron, and ramosetron were more efective compared to
early vomiting and vomiting within 24 hours. The treatment
efect of droperidol was associated with uncertainty and was
slightly worse for early vomiting and vomiting within 24 hours.
Dexamethasone and ondansetron showed similar treatment
efects at all time points investigated for vomiting. For nausea
within 24 hours, treatment efects of the NK1 receptor antagonists,
fosaprepitant and aprepitant, were associated with uncertainty

Overall completeness and applicability of evidence
Types of participants
Most of the studies in the current review included participants
at moderate to high risk for PONV based on patient-specific,
anaesthesia- and surgery-related risk factors. Most participants
were women (83%), received perioperative opioids (88%), were
undergoing general anaesthesia using volatile anaesthetics (88%),
and were subject to gynaecological or gastrointestinal surgery
(53%). The results of the review have limited external validity
with respect to the broad population of adults undergoing any
surgery with general anaesthesia but are directly transferable to
patients at risk for PONV (i.e. women undergoing gynaecological/
gastrointestinal surgery with volatile anaesthesia and with the
use of perioperative opioids). External validity is further limited
in that a majority of trials were conducted in inpatient settings
and included healthy participants classified as American Society of
Anesthesiologists status ASA I and II (70%). There was at least some
geographic variation in study locations, but most of the studies
were conducted in Asia (51%), Europe (25%), and North America
(16%).
Outcomes
We have chosen vomiting instead of nausea as the primary
outcome for this review because vomiting is an objectively
measurable outcome and may be associated with higher risk of
complications for the postoperative patient compared to nausea.
Nevertheless, several other PONV outcomes such as nausea and
complete response were also examined as secondary outcomes
in this review. However, depending on the outcome of interest,
there should be an altered risk/benefit assessment of some
antiemetics due to diferent efect profiles. For example, NK1
receptor antagonists have a better efect against vomiting than
against nausea and therefore do better in this review with a focus on
vomiting. In general, the main focus of this review should be on the
side efects of antiemetics, as the benefits of antiemetics have been
reported much better in the community than their side efects.
Eficacy
With this review, we found suficient available information to
address the review questions on eficacy of antiemetic drugs for
prevention of vomiting within 24 hours postoperatively. We found
high-certainty evidence showing that five single drugs (aprepitant,
ramosetron, granisetron, dexamethasone, and ondansetron)
reduce vomiting, and moderate-certainty evidence indicating that
two other single drugs (fosaprepitant and droperidol) probably
reduce vomiting compared to placebo. Consequently, four of the
six substance classes (5-HT3 receptor antagonists, D2 receptor
antagonists, NK1 receptor antagonists, and corticosteroids) were
represented by at least one single drug with high or moderate
certainty of evidence and important benefit for prevention of
vomiting. In absolute numbers, for 1000 patients, of whom 300
would vomit afer surgery if given placebo, 282 would benefit
from fosaprepitant (the most efective drug of the seven most
reliable single drugs) and 18 would not, or 117 would benefit from
droperidol (the least efective drug of the seven most reliable single
drugs) and 183 would not.
Safety and adverse events
In contrast to the large number of studies (89%) reporting relevant
eficacy outcomes for this review, just over half of all studies (56%)
reported at least one relevant safety outcome. Thus, relevant safety
outcomes were highly underrepresented in the included studies.
Furthermore, we could not exclude a certain risk of bias, as side
efects may be prone to selective outcome reporting and may have
been reported more frequently when the findings were generally
positive. In this NMA, the risk of selective outcome reporting was
dificult to assess, as we found few studies with a prospectively
registered protocol. In addition, most of the investigated side
efects occurred at a lower rate compared to the rate of PONV
(with the exception of the composite safety outcome ‘any AE’, which

There were two additional issues with adverse events. First, a
detailed definition of adverse outcomes such as QT prolongation
by study authors ofen was not available, was dificult to assess, or
was diferent between studies. In addition, the composite outcome
‘any AE’ was most ofen given as the total number of participants
with any adverse events. However, a detailed definition of which
outcomes were finally included ofen was not provided. Therefore,
the separated individual side efects such as headache were more
specific and informative. Second, study authors reporting the
composite outcome ‘any AE’ ofen gave insuficient information on
the method of monitoring adverse events. In most studies, it is
unclear whether researchers have actively surveyed participants
and have asked for the occurrence of any adverse event, or whether
they have used only information derived from routinely assessed
patient records or have focused only on specific adverse events,
lacking relevant side efects.
Interventions
This review compared 44 single drugs belonging to six diferent
substance classes. Twenty-one of the 44 drugs were of direct
interest, all of which are listed in the consensus guidelines
for management of postoperative nausea and vomiting (Gan
2014), with exception of the two newer drugs, fosaprepitant and
amisulpride. An additional 23 drugs were not of direct interest
and were used only to supplement the analysis. Drugs not
of direct interest were investigated in only 7% of all included
studies, limiting the gain of additional information and reflecting
the lack of importance of these drugs in clinical practice. The
current review is clearly dominated by three single drugs of direct
interest: ondansetron (with 246 studies), dexamethasone (with
120 studies), and droperidol (with 97 studies). Of the 21 single
drugs of direct interest, only meclizine was not investigated as a
single drug for any of the outcomes of interest. It was investigated
only in combination with ondansetron. Methylprednisolone and
perphenazine, used as single drugs, were not investigated for
the primary outcome of vomiting. Fosaprepitant and rolapitant
were not investigated for any of the relevant safety outcomes.
Dexamethasone, ondansetron, and tropisetron were present in
all outcomes investigated in this review. Finally, on the level of
substance classes, the 5-HT3 receptor antagonists were the largest
and the best investigated substance class in this review.
Included studies were published between 1965 and 2017. However,
most included studies (71%) were published in the last two decades
between 2000 and 2017. Despite the large amount of information
reported from clinical trials on this topic, the flood of clinical
trials was increasing over time, reaching a peak in 2007 with
36 published trials. Since 1996, more than 15 study reports per
year were published (Figure 4). On the one hand, there were new
substances, such as amisulpride and fosaprepitant, which have
been investigated only in recent trials. On the other hand, there
were several old and well-known drugs, such as ondansetron,
dexamethasone, and droperidol, that have been used extensively
in previous studies. However, they have also been studied in
recent studies. The use of ondansetron, the gold standard in PONV
clinical trials, has its justification in newer studies as an active
comparator. However, other recent studies—Zhang 2013-1; Zhang
2013-2—compared ondansetron against placebo and provided
no new or additional valuable findings compared to the large
IMPACT trial published in 2004 (Apfel 2004-1; Apfel 2004-2). Studies
that investigate what we already know and do not add any
clinically relevant information are not useful and should be avoided
(Ioannidis 2016).
Combination therapy
Combination therapy for PONV prophylaxis is preferable to
use of single drugs alone in patients at moderate risk (Gan
2014). Ondansetron, dexamethasone, and droperidol, for example,
have similar eficacy for PONV prophylaxis and, when used in
combination, they showed additive efects due to independent
mechanisms of action (Apfel 2004-1; Apfel 2004-2). In this
review, in addition to single drugs, any drug combination was
included, and this resulted in the inclusion of 51 diferent drug
combinations. In total, 28% of studies included drug combinations
and 72% of all studies investigated single drugs only. Thus,
evidence for the efectiveness of drug combinations in this
review was based on substantially fewer studies than for single
drugs alone. Nevertheless, 29 (81%) of 36 drug combinations
investigating the prevention of vomiting within 24 hours showed
important treatment efects based on NMA. Dexamethasone-
ondansetron (in 54 studies), dexamethasone-granisetron (in 20
studies), and droperidol-ondansetron (in 15 studies) are the only
drug combinations included in this review that were investigated
in more than 10 studies. Testing the additivity assumption for
prevention of vomiting within 24 hours revealed additive efects
of single drugs for these three combinations. Altogether, all
three combinations were equally efective in preventing vomiting
within 24 hours, with comparable efectiveness to aprepitant
administered as a single drug.
Combination treatments should include drugs of diferent
substance classes with diferent mechanisms of action (Gan 2014).
This recommendation is based on a strong biological rationale
without proof in clinical studies, as combinations of drugs from the
same substance class were not investigated in practice. Besides this
biological rationale, several findings on NMA treatment efects for
other eficacy outcomes (e.g. nausea) and adverse efects of single
drugs supported the use of combinations of drugs from diferent
substance classes. First, the NK1 receptor antagonists showed
promising antiemetic eficacy, whereas anti-nausea eficacy was
less prominent and was associated with uncertainty. In contrast,
the 5-HT3 receptor antagonists ramosetron and granisetron
and the D2 receptor antagonist droperidol efectively reduced
nausea. Therefore, ramosetron, granisetron, and droperidol might

Applicability of doses, administration routes, and application
time points
For the primary network meta-analyses, diferent doses,
administration routes, and application time points of individual
drugs were pooled together. Administration routes and application
time points were recorded in the Characteristics of included studies
section but were not analysed in detail in this review. Dose
efects were investigated in a subgroup analysis for vomiting,
splitting doses of drugs into dose categories in accordance with
current recommendations (Gan 2014). This review shows that low
doses of granisetron, ondansetron, dexamethasone, droperidol,
and tropisetron were less efective compared to recommended
and high doses. Because recommended and high doses of these
drugs were similarly efective, we assume recommended doses to
be suficient to prevent vomiting. No dose efects were detectable
for the other drugs, and we are best advised to use the most
investigated doses of drugs as the most reliable current guide. With
respect to recommendations of the current guideline, casopitant,
palonosetron, ramosetron, rolapitant, and tropisetron were most
ofen used at recommended doses according to Gan 2014 in this
systematic review. However, most of the studies investigating
aprepitant, dolasetron, haloperidol, and promethazine used high
doses, and most of the studies investigating dimenhydrinate
and metoclopramide used low doses. In these cases, dose
recommendations should be reconsidered, or additional studies
should investigate dose efects of these drugs. Ongoing debate
focuses on the topic of whether metoclopramide is efective for
prevention of PONV and whether its limited efectiveness may be
caused by low dosing schemes (DeOliveira 2012; Wallenborn 2006).
For amisulpride, fosaprepitant, and scopolamine, the current
guidelines did not give any dose recommendations (Gan 2014). In
the current systematic review, amisulpride was most ofen used at
a dose of 5 mg (IV, at induction of anaesthesia), fosaprepitant at 150
mg (IV, at induction of anaesthesia), and scopolamine at 1.5 mg (TD,
at induction of anaesthesia).
Interventions in current practice
The seven most efective single drugs for prevention of
postoperative vomiting with at least moderate-certainty evidence
found in this review vary by the level of establishment and
use in current practice. Ondansetron is the most used gold
standard antiemetic drug worldwide developed in the 1980s and
approved by the US FDA since January 1991. Dexamethasone
was developed in 1957 and was approved for medical use in
1961. It is listed together with ondansetron and metoclopramide
as an antiemetic medicine in the World Health Organization
List of Essential Medicines reporting the most efective and safe
medicines needed in a health system (WHO Model List of Essential
Medicines 2019). Droperidol was developed in the 1950s as an
antipsychotic and was first approved in Denmark in 1963 for use in
anaesthesia, PONV, and psychiatry. In the United States, droperidol
was withdrawn from clinical use in 2001 (FDA black box warning)
due to accumulating evidence of QT prolongation and concerns
about the risk of torsades de pointes (Sneyd 2009). Recently it has
been re-licensed in Europe for prevention and treatment of PONV
at lower doses of 0.625 to 1.25 mg in adults, and for prevention
of nausea and vomiting during postoperative patient-controlled
analgesia (PCA) in adults. Granisetron was developed in 1988 and
was approved in the UK in 1991 and in the United States in 1994
by the FDA. Ramosetron is approved for use only in Japan and
in certain Southeast Asian countries for treatment of nausea and
vomiting and diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome in
males (https://www.drugbank.ca/drugs/DB09290). Aprepitant was
approved for medical use in Europe and the United States in 2003.
It is listed on the complementary list of antiemetic medicines
in the World Health Organization List of Essential Medicines
(WHO Model List of Essential Medicines 2019). Fosaprepitant was
approved in 2008 by the FDA for use in combination with other
antiemetics for prevention of nausea and vomiting caused by
chemotherapy. Unlike aprepitant, fosaprepitant is approved by the
FDA for prevention of PONV.
Quality of the evidence
Certainty of evidence
This review includes a large number of studies (585 RCTs and 97,516
participants) with a large number of interventions (44 single drugs
and 51 drug combinations). Grading the certainty of evidence for
all possible combinations of interventions would be dificult to
conduct in a reasonable time frame and would be challenging
to present in an accessible manner. As an example, for vomiting
within 24 hours with 65 diferent treatments, a total of 2080 pair-
wise combinations of treatments were possible. This would equate
to 2080 evaluations of the certainty of evidence, which would be
an almost unmanageable task and would yield an overload of
information. Therefore, we decided to limit the assessment of the
certainty of evidence to single drugs of direct interest compared
to placebo. As a limitation of this review, an assessment of the
certainty of evidence for all drug combinations and all active
comparisons is not available.
Study quality based on risk of bias assessments
The overall methodological quality of the primary studies assessed
by the Cochrane risk of bias assessment tool 1.0 was limited
(Higgins 2011). Only 27% of the studies were assessed as having
overall low risk of bias. Most of the studies completely reported
their outcome data, which was feasible due to the short follow-
up intervals of the study. Major quality concerns were related to
selection bias, performance and detection bias, reporting bias, and
the other bias domain. About half of all studies did not report the
method used for randomization, and 88% of the studies did not
specify how allocation of participants was concealed to recruiters.
Blinding of participants, personnel, and outcome assessors was not
suficiently described in about 40% of all studies, and about 10%
had a non-blinded study design. Selective outcome reporting could
be assessed only for studies that had published a prospectively
registered study protocol. In total, only 5% of all included studies
had a prospectively registered study protocol, and only 2% were
judged to have low risk of selective outcome reporting. In the end,
we used information from the risk of bias assessment for sensitivity
analyses and interpretation of the certainty of evidence for all
relevant outcomes. For vomiting within 24 hours, suficient studies

Imprecision
For the primary eficacy outcome postoperative vomiting
within 24 hours, high-certainty evidence shows that five single
drugs (aprepitant, ramosetron, granisetron, dexamethasone, and
ondansetron) reduce vomiting, and moderate-certainty evidence
indicates that two other single drugs (fosaprepitant and droperidol)
probably reduce vomiting compared to placebo. For most of
the primary (SAE, any AE) and secondary safety outcomes
(headache, sedation, extrapyramidal symptoms, constipation,
wound infection, arrhythmia, QT prolongation, and visual
disturbances), we found only very low- to low-certainty evidence for
the efects of single drugs of direct interest compared to placebo.
Only a few exceptions are listed under Summary of main results.
One of the main reasons for the diferent certainty of evidence
levels for drugs in terms of eficacy and safety outcomes was the
diferent amount of underlying information in the NMAs (studies
and participants) combined with the lower baseline risks of most
safety outcomes. Therefore, the certainty of evidence for safety
outcomes is limited for most single drugs of direct interest as a
result of imprecision.
We used a clinically relevant size of efects—not statistical
significance—to describe and interpret network meta-analysis
estimates (Nikolakopoulou 2019; Wasserstein 2019). A risk ratio
(RR) of 0.8, which is equivalent to a relative risk reduction (RRR) of
20%, was assumed as a clinically relevant efect for vomiting, and
an RR of 0.9 (RRR 10%) was assumed as a clinically relevant efect
for all side efects. It is an advantage that precise efect estimates,
which are small (and clinically not relevant) but statistically
significant in a traditional sense, were not necessarily classified as
having a relevant efect. If such small and precise efect estimates
were located in the range of equivalence (RR 0.8 to 1.25 for
vomiting), they were classified as clinically not important. Only
efect estimates that were completely below an RR of 0.8 (benefit)
or above an RR of 1.25 (harm) were considered clinically relevant.
Moreover, intermediate stages of efect estimates might allow an
interpretation of imprecision reflecting the uncertainty associated
with efect estimates when 95% confidence intervals (CIs) are
broad and include diferent ranges. Furthermore, retiring statistical
significance and focusing on clinically relevant efect sizes helps
to solve issues associated with multiple testing in NMA (Efhimiou
2019).
Indirectness
All studies included in this review were relevant for the research
question in terms of our defined population, interventions,
comparisons, outcomes, and settings of interest. Our PICO criteria
are very specific, and all of the conclusions that we have drawn
in this review have been directly related to our research question.
Consequently, there were no concerns of indirectness in this
review, and the certainty of evidence was not downgraded for this
item. However, the CINeMA (Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis)
approach further considers an imbalance in the distribution
of efect-modifying variables among diferent comparisons for
the assessment of indirectness (Nikolakopoulou 2019; Salanti
2014). Efect modifiers are characteristics that impact the relative
treatment efect. Comparisons in NMAs will provide direct evidence
only if efect modifiers are equally distributed across studies and
comparisons. In this case, the assumption of transitivity holds in
the NMA. In the protocol, we defined diferences in sources of
funding, diferences in risk of bias, and diferences in details of
the interventions as efect-modifying variables relevant for this
review. In contrast, risk factors for PONV are prognostic variables
that directly afect the outcome but not the relative treatment efect
on the outcome. In the final review, we accepted heterogeneity
(see inclusion criteria of this review) for the efect modifiers ‘risk
of bias’ and ‘dose of intervention’. We have, however, assessed the
impact of these efect modifiers in sensitivity analyses (risk of bias)
and subgroup analyses (dose). Due to the quantity of data and the
lack of information for the efect modifier ‘funding source’ in many
studies, an objective and reliable assessment of the distribution
of this efect modifier within all comparisons was not possible.
In general, we assumed that for all included studies, the study
populations, interventions, outcomes, and study settings matched
the inclusion criteria of the current systematic review and were
suficiently similar. We have, however, accepted heterogeneity for
risk of bias and for intervention details. Thus, we concluded that
there was no relevant clinical and methodological heterogeneity
within and across treatment comparisons (intransitivity) in the
current review.
Heterogeneity and inconsistency/incoherence
In the entire network, there was heterogeneity within designs
for the primary eficacy outcome of vomiting. For all other
safety outcomes, no heterogeneity between studies of individual
comparisons was detectable. At the level of individual comparisons
of direct interest (single drugs of direct interest compared to
placebo), we assessed heterogeneity using the 95% prediction
interval (PI) and considered the impact on clinical conclusions
(Nikolakopoulou 2019). In the case of heterogeneity, we
investigated the efect-modifier dose in a subgroup analysis
and accepted a clinically relevant diference between doses as
an explanation for heterogeneity. If there was no explanation
by diferent doses of the intervention, we downgraded due
to heterogeneity. In the case of vomiting, heterogeneity
was detectable for comparisons of ondansetron, tropisetron,
dolasetron, droperidol, amisulpride, and dexamethasone—
all compared to placebo. Recommended and high doses
of ondansetron, droperidol, and dexamethasone were more
favourable compared to low doses. Thus, the certainty of evidence
for these comparisons could be applied only to recommended and
high doses. Most of the comparisons included in safety outcomes
appeared not heterogeneous, as the imprecision of efect estimates
was already large.
In the entire network, there was inconsistency between designs
for the primary eficacy outcome of vomiting. However, the full
random-efects design-by-treatment interaction model revealed
that there was no evidence of residual statistical inconsistency,
which means that all interventions behave similarly in all
comparisons. Other safety outcomes showed no inconsistency
between designs. At the level of individual comparisons of direct
interest (single drugs of direct interest compared to placebo),
we assessed incoherence by comparing direct and indirect efect
estimates with respect to impact on the clinical conclusion
(Nikolakopoulou 2019). In cases where both estimates have
