Publication bias
Publication bias was investigated by explorative analyses for direct
comparisons when 10 or more studies were included. Results
of the explorative analyses were dificult to interpret because
assessment of funnel plots is in general highly subjective, tests
for funnel plot asymmetry have low power, and several factors
other than publication bias may cause asymmetry in funnel
plots. With respect to these limitations, we decided to assume a
clinically relevant publication bias if the trim and fill sensitivity
analysis changed the clinical conclusion. The trim and fill sensitivity
analysis hypothetically estimates the efect based on missing
information of the asymmetrical studies. For the primary outcome
of vomiting, publication bias was suspected only for droperidol
for all single drugs of direct interest compared to placebo. In
the cases of dexamethasone, granisetron, and ondansetron (all
compared to placebo), the contour-enhanced funnel plots also
showed asymmetry. However, trim and fill did not change the
conclusion. In cases of granisetron and ondansetron, although
estimated efects were overestimated, they were still robust in
terms of the range of equivalence. Other primary and secondary
safety outcomes included too few studies to test for publication
bias, and in cases with enough studies, no publication bias was
suspected.
Ranking of treatments
We have reported ranking of treatments in terms of eficacy
and safety. The ranking of treatments is based on P scores
that measure the extent of certainty that a treatment is better
than another treatment, averaged over all competing treatments
(Rücker 2015). However, this statistical certainty should not be
confused with certainty of evidence. In this review, we have not
assessed the certainty of evidence for treatment rankings. In
cases where a large number of parameters were independently
estimated, the probability increases for finding some extreme
results that do not reflect reality (Efhimiou 2019). Thus, the ranking
of treatments should be interpreted with caution, and we want
to avoid overstated claims. However, comparing the extent of
an overlap of 95% CIs of diferent treatment comparisons may
enable us to get a better idea of clinically relevant diferences
between interventions. In the case of vomiting with placebo as the
reference compound, the NK1 receptor antagonists (fosaprepitant,
casopitant, and aprepitant) were the top three ranked single drugs
of direct interest. They were comparably efective to most of the
drug combinations, and their 95% CIs did not overlap with most of
the other single drugs of direct interest. This is a strong indicator
that NK1 receptor antagonists are the most efective single drugs
for prevention of vomiting. Diferences between all other drugs are
of minor importance. In case of most safety outcomes, the ranking
of drugs is highly unreliable due to excessive uncertainty in the
relative efects.
Potential biases in the review process
The feasibility of conducting an NMA including all available
interventions to prevent PONV in adults afer surgery strongly
correlates with the number of included studies. At the protocol
stage, we expected to include more than 1000 studies. Therefore,
we carefully planned the best way to narrow down the inclusion
criteria of this review to restrict the number of eligible studies
in advance. We restricted the review to the population of
adults undergoing general anaesthesia only, to pharmacological
interventions with direct antiemetic action, and to randomized
controlled trials published as full text. Thus we excluded all
abstracts and conference proceedings (a total of 84 studies)
from the current review. In a currently ongoing project, we used
these excluded studies as well as further studies found in an
additional search for abstract publications published in conference
proceedings to assess the potential for the loss of this information
(Hackenbroich (manuscript in preparation)). However, preliminary
results indicated that eligibility of most of these abstracts (about
85%) cannot be classified due to missing information. Thus, poor
reporting in abstract publications in the field of clinical PONV
research seems to be a general limitation preventing inclusion into
systematic reviews with narrow inclusion criteria. In contrast to the
exclusion of abstract publications, we wanted to include all RCTs
independent of their published language. In total, 83 (14%) of all
included studies were not published in English. As a strength of this
review, we included many local studies that were internationally
conducted in non-English-speaking countries. Furthermore, we
included full study reports that were not presented as a journal
publication. Eligible studies were found in clinical trial registries,
and full study reports were either directly linked or found on the
companies’ websites (e.g. GSK study register). Full study reports are
highly valuable and contain detailed information on study details,
especially safety assessments.
Several studies had duplicate publications in diferent journals
and were listed in trial registries under diferent first authors;
this complicated the process of data synthesis. By making the
dataset fully and freely available, we welcome perusal by outside
researchers to identify mistakes in our dataset, our analysis or our
interpretation.
A total of 185 studies identified in the first search were listed
as awaiting classification; these were either full-text publications
(86 studies) or study protocols (99 studies). No full texts for
screening and eligibility assessment could be retrieved for 29
studies. Insuficient reporting or lack of reporting of study details
relevant for the inclusion/exclusion decision was the main reason
for the inability to classify studies. Requests to study authors
remained unanswered in these cases. In a worst-case scenario, if
we assume that all 86 studies (awaiting classification) published
as full text would have been eligible for this review, then we have
currently lost about 10% of all available information to date due to
poor reporting. However, about half of the studies published as full
text and listed as awaiting classification were of older dates (date
of publication before 2000). Therefore, we assume that inclusion of
these studies would not have substantially altered the conclusions
of this review. In contrast, the multitude of studies published only
as study protocols and with pending classification were of later
publication dates. Future inclusion of these studies could alter the
conclusions of the review.
The review team conducting abstract and full-text screening, data
extraction, and critical appraisal consisted of 11  persons with
diferent background knowledge in conducting systematic reviews.

Agreements and disagreements with other studies or
reviews
A MEDLINE search for ‘postoperative nausea and vomiting’ AND
‘systematic review OR meta-analysis’ revealed more than 500
records (November 2019). This snapshot of the literature showed
not only that a large number of clinical trials have focused on
PONV research but also that a relatively large number of systematic
reviews have focused on this topic. In the following discussion, we
limit the critical comparison of our most important findings to two
large and well-known systematic reviews—the Carlisle Review at
Carlisle 2006a, and the Tricco Review at Tricco 2015a and Tricco
2015b.
The previous Cochrane Review on drugs for prevention of PONV
by Carlisle and Stevenson included RCTs investigating any drug
for prevention of PONV in participants of any age undergoing
general anaesthesia, regional anaesthesia, or sedation (Carlisle
2006a). This review searched several databases and included
737 studies involving 103,237 participants. Data were analysed
using pair-wise meta-analyses for PONV-related outcomes and
side efects comparing a drug with placebo or with another drug.
Risk of bias in studies was assessed. However, the certainty of
evidence was not evaluated. This review found eight drugs that
efectively prevent postoperative nausea and vomiting compared
to placebo: droperidol, metoclopramide, ondansetron, tropisetron,
dolasetron, dexamethasone, cyclizine, and granisetron. The risk
ratio (RR) versus placebo varied between 0.60 and 0.80, depending
upon the drug and the outcome. This review concluded that
publication bias made the evidence for diferences among these
drugs unreliable. Evidence for side efects was sparse: droperidol
was a sedative (RR 1.32), and headache was more common
afer ondansetron (RR 1.16). The Carlisle Review on PONV was
withdrawn in 2017, in part because this review included several
studies that were retracted since publication (Carlisle 2017). Our
review on prevention of PONV can be considered, to some extent,
as an update to the Carlisle Review. However, to enhance the
feasibility and conclusiveness of our review, we narrowed down
the inclusion criteria when compared to the Carlisle review and
included only adult participants undergoing general anaesthesia
who received an antiemetic intervention belonging to one of the
six relevant pharmacological substance classes for prevention of
PONV. This enabled us to focus the research question and to
limit the number of eligible RCTs. In addition, we used NMA
to compare all available drugs and combinations against each
other, thereby enabling us to generate a ranking of treatment
eficacy. Our review included some newer drugs compared to the
Carlisle Review, which are drugs of the NK1 receptor antagonist
class (aprepitant, casopitant, fosaprepitant, and rolapitant), and
some of the D2 receptor antagonists (amisulpride and haloperidol).
The current review selected the best drugs based on both an
important benefit for prevention of vomiting and moderate to
high certainty evidence. In contrast, the Carlisle Review selected
drugs that had an efect (95% CI < 1) on all four eficacy
outcomes (vomiting, nausea, nausea or vomiting, and rescue
antiemetic) without knowledge of the certainty of evidence. Four
of the eight drugs found to be preventive for PONV in the
Carlisle Review were also efective in preventing vomiting (with
moderate- to high-certainty evidence) in the current review—
dexamethasone, droperidol, granisetron, and ondansetron. We
found three more efective drugs with moderate- to high-certainty
evidence—aprepitant, fosaprepitant, and ramosetron. However,
the other four efective drugs found in the Carlisle Review were
not included in our review (cyclizine), were of only low-certainty
evidence (dolasetron and tropisetron), or were less efective and
of very low-certainty evidence (metoclopramide). The Carlisle
Review emphasized that publication bias makes evidence on
these drugs unreliable, especially for droperidol, ondansetron,
and granisetron. In contrast to the Carlisle Review, we excluded
all fraudulent studies and used an alternative strategy to assess
publication bias. In our review, we also suggested publication bias
for droperidol compared to placebo for vomiting. For granisetron
and ondansetron compared to placebo, although estimated NMA
treatment efects seem to be overestimated, the estimates were
still robust in terms of the clinical conclusion. Thus, we assume
that estimated treatment efects for granisetron and ondansetron
were overestimated due to publication bias; however, this does not
alter the conclusion. The Carlisle Review found sparse evidence for
side efects, and we thoroughly underscore this statement more
than 10 years later. Evidence for side efects remains limited. We
also found an increase in headache for ondansetron compared to
placebo with moderate-certainty evidence. We did not, however,
find a sedative efect of droperidol compared to placebo found by
the Carlisle Review.
A large NMA on the comparative eficacy and safety of 5-HT3
receptor antagonists compared to each other or placebo and/or
combined with other antiemetics for patients undergoing surgical
procedures was published in 2015 (Tricco 2015a; Tricco 2015b).
Tricco´s review had broader inclusion criteria than our review
in terms of the population of interest and the study design.
The Tricco Review included RCTs and non-randomized trials
investigating participants of any age undergoing any surgery with
any type of anaesthesia. However, the interventions of interest

searched several databases and included 450 studies with 80,410
participants for eficacy analyses (Tricco 2015a), along with 120

of bias was assessed, but certainty of evidence was not evaluated.

investigated drug relative to placebo, except for palonosetron plus
dexamethasone. Tricco and associates concluded that granisetron
plus dexamethasone was the most efective antiemetic. In
contrast, our review included many more combinations of 5-

A U T H O R S '   C O N C L U S I O N S
Implications for practice
•
We found high-certainty evidence showing that compared to
placebo, five single drugs (aprepitant, ramosetron, granisetron,
dexamethasone, and ondansetron) reduce vomiting, and
moderate-certainty evidence indicating that another two single
drugs (fosaprepitant and droperidol) probably reduce vomiting.
These were the seven most reliable and most efective drugs
identified in this review. Therefore, four of the six substance
classes (5-HT3 receptor antagonists, D2-receptor antagonists,
NK1-receptor antagonists, and corticosteroids) with diferent
mechanisms of action are represented by at least one drug that
shows benefit in terms of preventing vomiting.
•
In absolute numbers, for every 1000 patients, of whom 300
would vomit afer surgery if given placebo, 282 would benefit
from fosaprepitant (the most efective drug of the seven most
reliable single drugs) and 18 would not. If droperidol were given
(the least efective drug of the seven most reliable single drugs),
117 patients would benefit and 183 would not. Aprepitant,
ramosetron, granisetron, dexamethasone, and ondansetron
were ranked between fosaprepitant and droperidol in terms of
their eficacy for prevention of vomiting.
•
Recommended and high doses of granisetron, dexamethasone,
ondansetron, and droperidol were similarly efective but were
more efective than low doses for prevention of vomiting. So far,
no dose efects are detectable for aprepitant, ramosetron, and
fosaprepitant.
•
Ranking of treatments shows that combinations of drugs were
generally more efective than the corresponding single drugs
in preventing vomiting. However, NK1 receptor antagonists
were the most efective drug class, and single NK1 receptor
antagonists (fosaprepitant, casopitant, aprepitant) were as
efective as most of the drug combinations.
•
Other single drugs of direct interest for prevention of
postoperative vomiting were of uncertain efect due to
very low- to low-certainty evidence (casopitant, tropisetron,
dolasetron), were less efective (amisulpride, promethazine), or
both (palonosetron, haloperidol, metoclopramide, rolapitant,
dimenhydrinate, scopolamine), compared to placebo.
•
For most of the single drugs of direct interest, we found
only very low- to low-certainty evidence for safety assessed
by the occurrence of SAEs and any AE. We found only
moderate-certainty evidence for granisetron and amisulpride
indicating that the drugs probably have little or no efect
on any AE compared to placebo, and low-certainty evidence
suggesting that dimenhydrinate and scopolamine may increase
the number of patients with any AE.
•
The certainty of evidence for most of the single drugs of
direct interest ranged between very low and low for drug
class-specific side efects (headache, constipation, wound
infection, extrapyramidal symptoms, sedation, arrhythmia, QT
prolongation, visual disturbances). An exception was moderate-
certainty evidence showing that ondansetron probably
increases headache and probably reduces sedation compared
to placebo. The latter efect was limited to recommended
and high doses of ondansetron. Droperidol probably reduces
headache compared to placebo. Dexamethasone has no
efect on sedation compared to placebo. Dimenhydrinate
probably increases sedation and scopolamine may increase
the risk for visual disturbances, both compared to placebo.
No studies considered substance class-specific side efects
for fosaprepitant, the most efective drug for prevention of
vomiting.
•
Results of the review have limited external validity for the
broad population of adults undergoing any surgery with
general anaesthesia, but they are directly applicable to patients
at risk for PONV (i.e. women undergoing gynaecological/
gastrointestinal surgery with volatile anaesthesia and patients
using perioperative opioids).
Implications for research
We no longer need these types of studies.
•
Aprepitant, 
ramosetron, 
granisetron, 
dexamethasone,
ondansetron, and droperidol compared with placebo and with
diferent other active comparators in several studies included in
the NMA for vomiting. We do not need further RCTs investigating
inactive or active comparisons of these six drugs in the
investigated population.
•
Currently, we have no need for further RCTs comparing other
single drugs versus placebo for prevention of postoperative
vomiting in the investigated population. Head-to-head
comparisons should be the way forward for new drugs.
Here we describe future research needs.
•
Fosaprepitant was compared only to ondansetron for
prevention of vomiting in three studies. There is limited
connectivity within the network of vomiting. Fosaprepitant
should be compared to other active drugs such as
granisetron, ramosetron, dexamethasone, or aprepitant to
further investigate its leading position as the most efective
single drug for prevention of vomiting as reported in this review.
In addition, no dose-response studies nor safety studies are
available for fosaprepitant in this context.
•
Data on the NK1 receptor antagonists casopitant and rolapitant
are limited, although this substance class shows promising anti-
vomiting efects.
•
The conclusions of this review are restricted to patients at risk
(women, patients undergoing gynaecological/gastrointestinal
surgery, patients given inhalational anaesthesia, and patients
using perioperative opioids), most of whom are healthy patients

more severe disease or patients in outpatient settings derive
benefit or harm from antiemetic prophylaxis is still unclear.
•
Most patients in the general surgical population exposed
to prophylactic antiemetics will not benefit because about
70% would not sufer from vomiting. Therefore, we need
to understand the risk of side efects. To increase the
chances of detecting even rare side efects (e.g. QT
prolongation, arrhythmia, extrapyramidal symptoms), non-
randomized cohort studies or systematic reviews including non-
randomized studies would be useful, in addition to RCTs.
•
We do not understand whether higher doses of drugs increase
the chances of sufering from certain side efects. Dose-response
studies on side efects or observational studies on dose efects
would be useful in this regard.
•
Future studies should report exact outcome definitions (e.g.
QT prolongation, arrhythmia, extrapyramidal symptoms) and
should fully report all investigated safety outcomes. Study
authors should use online repositories and supplementary
material to store detailed information.
•
All new studies should prospectively publish a study protocol
in an oficial trial registry. All outcomes of interest including
outcome definition, method to measure, and time points should
be listed.
•
New studies should provide a detailed description of baseline
characteristics and the distribution of classical risk factors for
PONV in the study population (e.g. in a supplementary table).
•
New RCTs should use and clearly describe methods for
allocation concealment.
•
All studies should declare their funding resources and potential
conflicts of interest.
•
Negative and non-significant results are also important. We call
on all investigators who conducted studies on PONV in the past
to please publish their studies, even if time has passed since
the study was conducted. Only in this way can we obtain an
unbiased picture of the benefits and harms of all relevant drugs.

Included criteria: elective surgery during general anaesthesia that was expected to last at least 1 hour,
risk of postoperative nausea and vomiting that exceeded 40% (presence of at least 2 of the following
risk factors: female sex, non-smoker status, previous history of postoperative nausea and vomiting or
motion sickness, anticipated use of postoperative opioids)
Excluded criteria: contraindication to any of the study drugs, had taken emetogenic or antiemetic
drugs within the 24 hours before surgery, expected to require postoperative mechanical ventilation,
pregnant or lactating
Pretreatment: baseline characteristics (age): no; (weight, BMI, ASA): unclear. Potential effect modi-
fiers (gender, duration of anaesthesia, non-smoker, history of PONV/motion sickness, perioperative
opioids): no

ues as specified by the protocol (alanine aminotransferase or aspartate aminotransferase > 2.5× upper

paroscopic cholecystectomy, or breast augmentation surgery with anticipated duration of 1 to 3 hours;

and postoperative opioids

tero-myoma, ovarian cyst, or other benign gynaecological disease; enucleation of benign tumour; la-
paroscopic surgery); gynaecological diagnostic laparoscopy; cholecystectomy under inhalation anaes-
thesia, alone or in combination with epidural anaesthesia; ASA I to III, preoperative physical status
Excluded criteria: severe hepatic, renal, cardiac, or pulmonary dysfunction or haemopoietic organ dis-
order; history of drug allergy or anaphylactic symptoms; gastrointestinal transit disorder or active pep-
tic ulcer; brain tumour or epilepsy or receiving a psychotropic agent with an antiemetic effect; had ex-
perienced nausea and/or vomiting during the 24 hour period before administration of the study med-
ication; had received another study drug within 3 months of starting the study; were due to use anoth-
er investigational drug concurrently; had undergone radiotherapy or chemotherapy within the 24 hour
period before dosing with the study medication; were due to undergo radiotherapy or chemotherapy
during the observation period; were pregnant or nursing; might be, or wished to be, pregnant within 30
days of receiving the study medication

Included criteria: 20 to 55 years of age, ASA I or II, scheduled for elective laparoscopic surgical proce-
dure with known high risk of PONV. Risk factors were female gender, non-smoking status, history of
PONV or motion sickness, and postoperative opioids. Each risk factor was given a score of 1. Only pa-
tients who had at least 2 risk factors (risk score 2 to 4) were enrolled
Excluded criteria: over 60 years of age, ASA > III, body mass index (BMI) > 35 kg/m2, received a prophy-
lactic antiemetic within 24 hours of surgery, concomitant administration of steroids or psychotropic
drugs, contraindication to the use of corticosteroids (glaucoma, severe hypertension, heart disease, re-
nal failure, peptic ulcer disease, diabetes mellitus, adrenal insufficiency, immunosuppression, recent
tuberculosis), pregnant or lactating women, a condition requiring long-term opioid use, allergic to any
of the study drugs (excluded and replaced by other patients)

Included criteria: female, known risk factors for PONV, undergoing gynaecological or gallbladder
surgery, ASA I or II
1. Female with the following 3 risk factors:
- premenopausal or perimenopausal between the ages of 18 and 55 years, not of childbearing potential
(i.e. physically incapable of becoming pregnant), demonstrating a negative serum or a negative urine
pregnancy test within 24 hours before the first administration of study medication and agrees to:
- abstain from sexual intercourse for 2 weeks before administration of the first dose of study medica-
tion until 30 days after the final dose of study medication, or
- use hormonal methods of birth control (e.g. oral, injectable, implantable) or other highly effective
method of contraception (e.g. an intrauterine device (IUD)) in conjunction with a barrier method of
contraception (condom, spermicidal foam, sponge, gel, diaphragm) if engaging in sexual intercourse
for at least 7 days before the first dose of study medication and continuing until 30 days after the final
dose of study medication
- have never smoked or used (e.g. chewing) tobacco (including nicotine patches) for the previous 12
months
- have a history of postoperative nausea and vomiting and/or motion sickness
2. Undergoing a laparoscopic/laparotomy gynaecological surgical procedure or laparoscopic cholecys-
tectomy that is scheduled for no less than 1 hour and no longer than 3 hours in duration. For the pur-
poses of this study, “scheduled” is considered the duration of time that the surgical suite is blocked for
the procedure (i.e. the operating room block time) or the duration of time in which it is anticipated that
the subject will be in the operative preparation/operating room
3. Scheduled to receive general anaesthesia with an anaesthetic regimen as described in the Anesthetic
Regimen (see Section 4.2., “Anesthetic and Analgesic Regimens”)
4. Meeting ASA Physical Status Classification of I or II preoperatively on the day of surgery

5. Having haematology and blood chemistry values within acceptable limits (i.e. within 10% outside (ei-
ther above or below) normal reference values, unless otherwise specified) for surgery, including, but
not limited to:
- haemoglobin, hematocrit, total white blood cell count, platelet counts
- alkaline phosphatase, blood urea nitrogen or serum urea, electrolytes (sodium, potassium, chloride,
bicarbonate)
- liver function tests (alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) < 1.5 times
the upper limit of normal), serum creatinine (< 1.5 times the upper limit of normal), total bilirubin (< 1.5
times the upper limit of normal)
6. Able and willing to complete daily components of the subject diary preoperatively on the day of
surgery and until the end of the 120-hour assessment period, and available to respond to follow-up by
study personnel at the 120-hour study period post emergence from anaesthesia
7. Understanding the nature and purpose of this study and the study procedures and signed an in-
formed consent form for this study to indicate this understanding
Excluded criteria:
1. Meeting ASA Physical Status Classification of III, IV, or V preoperatively on the day of surgery
2. Pregnant or lactating
3. Post-menopausal. If the last menstrual period was within the previous 18 months, a follicle-stim-
ulating hormone (FSH) evaluation in the postmenopausal range will satisfy that the subject is post-
menopausal
4. Scheduled to undergo only a laparoscopic biopsy
5. Scheduled to receive neuraxial anaesthesia (e.g. epidural, spinal, caudal anaesthesia) or total IV
anaesthesia
6. Scheduled to receive propofol for maintenance of anaesthesia
7. Scheduled to have gastric contents suctioned continuously during the surgical procedure via a naso-
gastric tube, or a nasogastric or oral gastric tube during the postoperative period. A single pass at the
beginning or at the end of the surgical procedure and intraoperative gastric suctioning of air are per-
mitted
8. Taking more than 10 mg to 15 mg of oxycodone, or an equivalent opioid dose, on a regular, daily ba-
sis, for more than 3 consecutive days in the week before surgery
9. Received an investigational drug in the previous 30 days or scheduled to receive any investigational
drug in addition to GW597599 during the study period
10. Persistent or recurrent nausea and/or vomiting due to other aetiologies, including, but not limited
to, gastric outlet obstruction, hypercalcaemia, active peptic ulcer, increased intracranial pressure, or
brain metastases
11. Experienced retching or vomiting or uncontrolled nausea within 48 hours before administration of
the GW597599 study medications
12. Experienced significant nausea in the 24-hour period before receiving the GW597599 study medica-
tions
13. Received radiation therapy to the abdomen or the pelvis in the seven days before receiving study
medications and/or will receive radiation therapy to the abdomen or the pelvis in the evaluation period
14. History of wound dehiscence
15. History of any other illness, which, in the opinion of the Investigator, may pose an unacceptable risk
when study medication is administered
16. Any current or past medical condition (e.g. vagotomy) and/or requiring medication to treat a condi-
tion that could confound evaluation of the data collected in this clinical trial
17. Known hypersensitivity or contraindication to ondansetron hydrochloride or ondansetron, anoth-
er 5-HT3 receptor antagonist, any scheduled anaesthetic or analgesic agents, or any component of
GW597599
18. Known hypersensitivity to fentanyl and/or ketorolac tromethamine
19. Known allergy to eggs or egg products (component of propofol)
20. Scheduled to receive antiemetics not outlined in the study dosing scheme
21. Received medication with known or potential antiemetic activity within the 24-hour period before
receiving study medications. This includes, but is not limited to:
- 5-HT3 receptor antagonists (e.g. ondansetron, granisetron, dolasetron, tropisetron, ramosetron).
Palonosetron is not permitted for 7 days before the study
- benzamide/benzamide derivatives (e.g. metoclopramide, alizapride)
- benzodiazepines (except if the subject is receiving such medication for sleep and has been on a stable
dose for at least 7 days before the first dose of study medication; however, lorazepam is prohibited)

Included criteria: men and women; 18 to 65 years of age; ASA I to III; considered at high risk for post-
operative nausea and vomiting; undergoing ambulatory plastic surgery under general anaesthesia of at
least 1 hour duration were eligible for this prospective, randomized, double-blind trial. Subjects were
recruited on the day of surgery during the preoperative evaluation by study investigators (M.C.V. and
R.C.R.), who were anaesthesiologists already involved in patient care. Major postoperative nausea and
vomiting patient-related risk factors for inclusion in this study were (1) female gender, (2) history of
postoperative complication or history of motion sickness, (3) non-smoking status, (4) postoperative
use of opioids. Patients with 2 or more risk factors were eligible for the study. All patients who were
scheduled for either outpatient or 23-hour observation were included in the study, as,depending on the
time of day, the 2 groups of patients were interchangeable
Excluded criteria: patient refusal to participate in the study, had received other antiemetics before
their procedure, history of allergy or sensitivity to study drugs, pregnancy, history of long-term opioid
use (chronic pain syndrome). Women of reproductive age were routinely screened for pregnancy; pa-
tients who were pregnant were informed and excluded from the study

Appendix 5. Criteria for GRADEing the quality of evidence
The certainty of the evidence was assessed by two independent reviewers for the following domains and according to the following criteria:
Within-study risk of bias (study limitations): the contribution matrix was used to approximate the contribution of each piece of study
to the NMA of relative treatment efects (Papakonstantinou 2018; Salanti 2014). A combination of study contributions with study risk of
bias assessments (high, unclear, and low risk of bias) was used to evaluate study limitations for each NMA of relative treatment efect. We
have assessed the quality level that contributed most to the NMA of treatment efect (majority RoB). In addition, we have compared the
results of the NMA including all studies (primary analysis) with those obtained when only low risk of bias studies were included (sensitivity

analysis). If the clinical impact between the primary and the sensitivity NMA of treatment efect with respect to the range of equivalence
does not difer (location of point estimate and 95% CI), no concern due to study limitations has been assumed.
Across-studies bias (publication bias): the risk of across-studies bias was investigated on the comparison level and only when a suficient
number of studies per direct comparison was available. For pair-wise comparisons with 10 or more relevant studies, we investigated risk
of bias across studies using funnel plots and contour-enhanced funnel plots. In addition, we performed exploratory analyses (e.g. Rücker’s
arcsine test for dichotomous data, trim and fill sensitivity meta-analysis) to further investigate funnel plot asymmetry. Based on these
empirical examinations, we assumed two possible descriptions for across-studies bias: undetected or suspected.
Indirectness: the domain indirectness refers to the relevance of the included studies to the research question. Among all reported studies,
study populations, interventions, outcomes, and study settings matched the inclusion criteria of the current systematic review. Thus, we
concluded that there is no indirectness in any of the studies included in the current review.
Imprecision: the 95% confidence interval expressed the uncertainty of the relative NMA treatment efects. Imprecise treatment efects
with a wide confidence interval may be associated with high uncertainty regarding the clinical decision. We considered the range of
treatment efects included in the confidence interval and compared it with the respective range of equivalence. The inclusion of diferent
clinical implications in the confidence interval indicates an imprecise NMA treatment efect, and down-rating for imprecision was required
(Nikolakopoulou 2019).
Heterogeneity: we measured heterogeneity using the 95% prediction interval, which indicates where the true efect of a future study
is expected to lie (Riley 2011). Similarly to imprecision, of highest importance for assessing NMA treatment efects with respect to
heterogeneity is whether a clinical decision is substantially influenced (Nikolakopoulou 2019). We evaluated compatibility between
confidence and prediction intervals in terms of the range of equivalence for the assessment of heterogeneity.
If heterogeneity was present, we investigated "dose of the intervention" as a potential efect modifier in a subgroup network meta-analysis.
Diferent clinical decisions between NMA treatment efects of low, recommended, and high doses with respect to the range of equivalence
were included in the final judgement on heterogeneity.
Incoherence: disagreement between direct and indirect evidence is termed incoherence. It cannot be tested in cases where only direct or
indirect evidence exists. However, if only indirect evidence is present, there is always some concern, and we downgraded the comparison
for incoherence (Nikolakopoulou 2019). In cases where more than 90% of the information comes from direct evidence, we assumed that
incoherence was not a concern (Salanti 2017).
In other cases, we used two ways of judging incoherence. First, we used a local test (ratio of risk ratios (direct versus indirect), test for
disagreement) to measure inconsistency. Because we recognized the low power of this test for inconsistency, as already described by
others, we considered the implication of incoherence for clinical decisions as an alternative (Nikolakopoulou 2019). Thus, we compared
the clinical interpretation of confidence intervals of direct and indirect efect estimates with respect to the range of equivalence
(Nikolakopoulou 2019). If direct and indirect estimates (95% CIs) were incoherent, we assessed whether both estimates contribute
importantly to the NMA treatment efect (Brignardello-Petersen 2019). The proportions of direct and indirect contributions to the NMA
treatment efect were calculated using König’s method provided by the R command netsplit in the R package netmeta. If direct and indirect
estimates contributed in a way comparable to 30% to 70% contribution to the NMA treatment efect, and if 95% CIs of both estimates were
diferent (incoherent) with respect to the range of equivalence, down-rating for incoherence was required. If there was a dominant estimate
(> 70% contribution) and the 95% CI was similar to the 95% CI of the NMA estimate, no down-rating for incoherence was performed.
Summarizing judgements across the six domains: we considered our judgements on separate domains in conjunction rather than in
isolation. We paid particular attention not to downgrade twice for the same aspect (Nikolakopoulou 2019). Salanti et al described the
following overlapping domains: indirectness – incoherence, heterogeneity – incoherence, heterogeneity – imprecision, and heterogeneity
– publication bias (Nikolakopoulou 2019). For overlapping domains, we downgraded only once.

•
Types of studies: we have planned in the protocol that eligible studies must be published in a peer-reviewed journal. We changed this
restriction and decided to include all studies that were published as full-text articles independent of a peer-review process. Peer review
may be one reason for publication bias (selective publication of positive and significant results).
•
Types of participants: we have defined in the protocol that we include adult participants (≥ 18 years) undergoing any type of surgery
under general anaesthesia. During full-text screening, we have recognized that many studies have not reported any eligibility criteria
or lower bound of age for study participants, or have used other definitions of “adults” starting with 15, 16, or 17 years. Because we are
interested in the adult population in the biological sense, we extended our inclusion criteria for age as follows: for each study enrolling
participants younger than 18 and reporting the mean age with SD, we assumed that a majority of participants are 18 or older, and that
the study is eligible for this review, when the lower bound of the confidence interval (mean age ± 1.5 SD) is 18 or greater (Chebyshev’s
inequality). Similarly, if the study reports the median and the IQR of age with the lower bound of the IQR 18 or greater, then we can state
that a majority of participants are 18 or older.
•
New secondary outcome: complete response (number of participants without vomiting, nausea, or need for rescue treatment within
24 hours postoperatively). Complete response is an important outcome for participants in the postoperative period.
•
Searching other resources: we have scanned the reference lists of included studies only of the following relevant systematic reviews
Carlisle 2006a; De Oliveira 2013; Liu 2015; Tricco 2015a; Tricco 2015b. We have not scanned the reference lists of all included studies in
the current review, and we have not contacted trial authors for further relevant studies in the field.
•
Overall risk of bias summary: we have summarized the risk of bias for each study depending on judgements for the items 'sequence
generation', 'blinding of participant, personnel, and outcome assessors', and 'incomplete outcome data'. At the protocol stage, we had
planned to use the item 'allocation concealment' instead of 'sequence generation'. However, we judged only 69 studies (12%) that
used either central allocation or sequentially numbered opaque sealed envelopes (SNOSE) as having low risk of bias for allocation
concealment. In contrast, a total of 282 studies (48%) have reported adequate methods for sequence generation such as random
numbers tables or computer-generated random numbers. We believe that most authors of previous studies were unaware of the
definition and reporting standards of methods for allocation concealment. Most study authors have reported on sequence generation
and blinding but not on allocation concealment. The term 'SNOSE' was used only in more recent studies. Therefore, we decided to use
'sequence generation' instead of 'allocation concealment', because we assume that allocation concealment may have worked in many
more studies included in this systematic review. Reporting of methods used for allocation concealment is the real problem.
•
Assessment of clinical and methodological heterogeneity within treatment comparisons: we had planned to use descriptive statistics as
reported in the Characteristics of included studies table to assess whether studies within each pair-wise comparison are homogenous
enough with respect to potential efect modifiers (risk of bias, intervention details, funding source), so that the assumption of
homogeneity might be plausible. Finally, for the efect modifiers ‘risk of bias’ and ‘dose of intervention’, we accepted heterogeneity (see
inclusion criteria of this review) and assessed the impact of these efect modifiers in either sensitivity analysis (risk of bias) or subgroup
analysis (dose). Due to the quantity of data and lack of information for the efect modifier ‘funding source’ in many studies, an objective
and reliable assessment of the distribution of this efect modifier within all comparisons was not possible. In general, we assumed
that for all included studies, the study populations, interventions, outcomes, and study settings matched the inclusion criteria of the
current systematic review. Thus, we concluded that there is no relevant clinical and methodological heterogeneity within treatment
comparisons in the current review.
•
Assessment of transitivity across treatment comparisons: we had planned to assess the assumption of transitivity by comparing
the distribution of potential efect modifiers (see data extraction form ‘Potential efect modifiers’) across the diferent pair-wise
comparisons. In case of intransitivity (e.g. substantially imbalanced distribution of efect modifiers among comparisons), we did not
want to perform NMA. Finally, for the efect modifiers ‘risk of bias’ and ‘dose of intervention’, we accepted diferences in the distribution
of these efect modifiers across treatment comparisons (see inclusion criteria of this review) and assessed the impact of these efect
modifiers in either sensitivity analysis (risk of bias) or subgroup analysis (dose). Due to the quantity of data and lack of information for
the efect modifier ‘funding source’ in many studies, an objective and reliable assessment of the distribution of this efect modifier within
all comparisons was not possible. In general, we assumed that for all included studies, the study populations, interventions, outcomes,
and study settings matched the inclusion criteria of the current systematic review. Thus, we concluded that there is no relevant clinical
and methodological heterogeneity across treatment comparisons (intransitivity) in the current review.
•
Net heat plot: to locate sources of inconsistency, we had planned to use net heat plots. However, data were too complex to visualize
net heat plots in a meaningful manner.
•
Subgroup analyses: in case of heterogeneity or inconsistency, we had planned to explore potential efect modifiers as possible sources.
Due to the complex nature of the review, we decided to perform only the subgroup analysis 'dose of the interventions'. In addition, we
have added a table summarizing the most commonly used dosages, routes, and time points of administration of single drugs of direct
interest for the primary outcome vomiting and have reported this information in the Efects of interventions section.
•
Methods for analysing additive dose efects: we have added the analysis to test the assumption whether the efects of combined dose
categories (e.g. low + recommended, low + recommended + high, recommended + high) are additive sums of their individual categories.
•
Reporting of efect estimates: we decided the process/method of selection of efect estimates for reporting in the Efects of interventions
section at the review stage afer performing the analyses. Selection was not driven by specific results.
•
Sensitivity analyses: we included two new sensitivity analyses on funding (funding source 'industry', funding source 'non-industry'). We
added one new sensitivity analysis on 'single drugs only' including only study arms investigating single drugs and excluding study arms
investigating combinations of drugs. This analysis compared the robustness of network efect estimates of the primary network meta-
analysis and the sensitivity analysis including single drugs only (which is the basic analysis for the subgroup analysis of dose).
